speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY-ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to advise the house that initial payments for the basic grades of western wheat, oats and barley have been approved by the government and established for the crop year 1961-62. These initial payments have been set at the same level as those in effect for the present crop year.
The initial payment for wheat, effective August 1 next, is $1.40 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern, in store Fort William-Port Arthur or Vancouver. The initial payment for oats is 60 cents per bushel, basis No. 2 Canada western, in store Fort William-Port Arthur. The initial payment for barley is 96 cents per bushel, basis No. 3 Canada western six-row, in store Fort William-Port Arthur.
For all other grades of wheat, oats and barley the initial payments effective for the 1961-62 crop year will be established at a later date on the recommendation of the Canadian wheat board.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN MAXIMUM QUOTA

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN MAXIMUM QUOTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to show the concern of the Canadian wheat board over the drought situation in the west and the steps being taken to alleviate this problem, I wish to make the following statement. I wish to inform the house that the Canadian wheat board has announced that the maximum quota for the present crop year will be 7 bushels per specified acre. The first authorizations for the quota at points where sufficient space is available to warrant the increase have already been issued to the trade.
For the balance of the crop year, in so far as possible the Canadian wheat board will endeavour to give all producers an opportunity to deliver the maximum quota. Therefore effective Monday, July 3, the key agent
at a delivery point where producers have had an opportunity to deliver a 6 bushel quota and where space is available to warrant an increase to 7 bushels per specified acre should, with the consent of the other agents at the point, request the quota department of the Canadian wheat board, Winnipeg, to authorize an increase to that level.
It should be understood, however, that in authorizing a 7 bushel quota at such delivery points the board does not undertake that sufficient space will be made available to enable all producers to deliver the maximum quota. The significance of this, Mr. Speaker, is that the responsibility of requesting the 7 bushel quota now rests with the elevator agents.

On the orders of the day:

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN MAXIMUM QUOTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture arising out of his answer this morning. I should like to break it down into three parts.
First, can the points of delivery take it that the minister's announcement is equivalent to a buying order for each point equal to 7 bushels? Second, what assurance have these elevator agents that box cars will be available for delivery? Third, what is the situation in the event that elevators of the key personnel to which he referred are full and the other elevators are empty or have storage space?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN MAXIMUM QUOTA
speechtext: Order paper.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN MAXIMUM QUOTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some difficulty in answering the first question, in so far as who is responsible. The main point of my statement was that once the 6-bushel quota has been granted by the wheat board the responsibility lies on the local agents to call for a 7-bushel quota.
We certainly cannot give assurance of box cars, but I think, with the co-operation we are getting from the railways and the terminals these days, we could meet pretty well all the requirements.
The third part of the hon. member's question about the key agent is a touchy one in western Canada. The key agent is usually the leading recipient of grain in that particular town. If his elevators happen to be full naturally he will tend not to request an additional quota. I think it is up to the other

Dominion-Provincial Relations agents to persuade him that they have space and that they should be able to get the cars. What we and the wheat board are really trying to do here is first of all to put the responsibility on the local elevator agents to decide whether or not grain should be moved out of that district; second, to put the responsibility on the agents to let the farmers know that the agents themselves decide whether they go to a 7-bushel quota.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN MAXIMUM QUOTA
speechtext: A supplementary question. The minister referred to those stations or points that were on a 6-bushel quota. As he well knows, many points in Saskatchewan are on a 5-bushel quota. Does the same thing apply to a 5-bushel quota?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN MAXIMUM QUOTA
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. I think the intention of the wheat board is that very shortly almost all points will be on the 6-bushel quota and we are assuming that the 6 bushels will be arrived at some time this week. From there on the local agents will have to decide whether they go up to 7 bushels.

On the order:
Consideration of the amendment made by the Senate to Bill C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff-the Minister of Finance.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, hon. members will not need to be reminded that Bill No. C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, is one of the bills introduced arising out of the supplementary budget presented to the house on December 20 last. It is a bill that received extended discussion in this house before proceeding to the other place.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I interrupt the minister for a moment? We do not have the amendment. I think the amendments are normally on the table.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the message of the Senate-
Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think we should have the amendment before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The amendment is before us, Mr. Speaker, and has been since June 15. The message of the Senate containing the amendment which is proposed by the other place was received by this house on June 15 and is recorded in Votes and Proceedings of this house of that date at page 671. This, of course, is the practice of the house. When Senate amendments come to the house they appear in Votes and Proceedings but are not transcribed in extenso on the order paper of this house.
At page 671 of Votes and Processings the following passage from the message from the Senate will be found:
A message was received from the Senate informing this house that the Senate had passed Bill No. C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, with the following amendment:
Page 1, lines 22 and 23: Strike out lines 22 and 23 and substitute therefor the following:
"(3) Subject only to an appeal to the tariff board, the decision of which board shall be final and in respect of which appeal the provisions of section 44 of the Customs Act shall apply mutatis mutandis, the minister shall decide the following matters:".
Hon. members accordingly will recognize that the Senate has proposed one amendment by which it is intended that a right of appeal in limited form should be extended; that such right of appeal should apply in the cases contemplated in Bill No. C-72; and that the appeal shall not be of the same nature as the appeal provisions now in effect, that is to say an appeal to the tariff board with further appeals in certain cases and on certain grounds to the exchequer court and the Supreme Court of Canada, but an appeal to the tariff board whose decision is to become final.
The issue therefore presented to the house is whether the house should accept or reject the Senate amendment. The government cannot accept it, and it asks the house therefore to reject the amendment proposed by the Senate.
Hon. members will not need to be reminded that the Customs Tariff is certainly a revenue statute. Bill No. C-72, to amend the Customs Tariff, is a fiscal measure. It was one of the budget bills. It is clearly a revenue bill. It is no answer to say that the particular amendment does not expressly relate in its terms to particular tax rates. The bill itself is a revenue measure. The main statute which it purports to amend is by any standard a revenue measure, a fiscal enactment.
I shall not delay the house, Mr. Speaker, by reminding it of the important place which this amending bill held in the government's program for enlargement of job opportunities in Canada, and of the stress that was laid

Customs Tariff
upon that fact in the earlier debates of this session. I am sure that matter is fresh in the minds of hon. members. I therefore turn directly to the question presented to us by the Senate amendment.
I have to say in general that the amendment is an unworkable one and that it would result in frustrating the purposes of the bill to which it purports to be an amendment. It would result in delays that I am sure the house could not possibly condone. I make these brief observations before proceeding to a leading element that challenges the house in the light of the action taken by the Senate. The suggested amendment is open to these criticisms.
1.	The delays and uncertainty which would be brought about by having the questions of "normal Canadian consumption", "shelf" goods and whether goods are "custom made to specifications" subject to an appeal to the tariff board may discourage Canadian producers from taking an active interest in such new business.
2.	Notwithstanding what has been said regarding how swiftly the tariff board might be expected to deal with such cases-indeed, Mr. Speaker, it was said that they could be disposed of within a period of 60 days-the bald fact is that on June 13, to take a recent date, the tariff board issued a tentative schedule for the hearing of appeals in November and December of this year and in February, April and June of 1962. Such is the extent of the backlog, and such is the measure of the delay that must result in the inscription of any more appeals or the creation of procedure for more appeals under our statutes.
Included among these cases which have already been set down for hearing in this group of appeals now standing for hearing up to June of 1962 are three involving class or kind rulings. These are listed for hearing eight months to 10 months hence. Appeal No. 599, which was accepted by the board in November, 1960, is scheduled for hearing in February, 1962, while appeals Nos. 600 and 606, which were accepted in November, 1960 and January, 1961 respectively, are listed for hearing in April, 1962.
3.	The anomaly of having a portion of the class or kind provisions subject to appeal to the tariff board only while other features of the legislation allow the filing of appeals beyond the board to the Exchequer Court of Canada and to the Supreme Court of Canada. This anomaly, I am sure, requires little further comment.
Under the amendment, first, the normal Canadian consumption of shelf goods; second, whether goods are custom made to specifications; and third, whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production

of custom made goods within a reasonable period of time would be appealable to the tariff board only. The questions which could be taken before the courts include, first, whether shelf goods are of approximately the same class or kind as goods made in Canada; second, the determination of the amount of Canadian production; and third, whether the quantity manufactured in Canada does in fact constitute a minimum of 10 per cent of normal Canadian consumption.
The fourth ground of criticism and the fourth reason why such an amendment would be quite unworkable and accordingly unacceptable is the possibility that the phrase "custom made to specifications" may be construed as applying to a much wider range of goods than is presently contemplated, such as articles which may merely differ in quality, capacity, size, style, etc.
These observations are all that I am sure I need to detain the house in mailing in order to point out the unworkability of the amendment proposed by the Senate. However, I should like to pass now to something which is fundamental and which in effect presents the house with an issue with important constitutional implications. The house is aware of the rule in regard to the prerogatives of this house respecting money bills. This is the problem presented now in relation to this present bill and the amendment proposed.
Rule 63 of the house, Mr. Speaker, which you applied on a previous occasion, reads as follows:
63. All aids and supplies granted to Her Majesty by the parliament of Canada, are the sole gift of the House of Commons, and all bills for granting such aids and supplies ought to begin with the house, as it is the undoubted right of the house to direct, limit, and appoint in all such bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which are not alterable by the Senate.
Mr. Speaker, that rule was applied by yourself to an amendment to the Income Tax Act proposed by the Senate in the 1959 session. It gave rise to debate in this house on July 14 and July 18 of that session. May I just remind hon. members of the circumstances of that occasion, because there we have a complete precedent created by this present parliament. We do not even need to go back to statements on the question in earlier parliaments, although there are a number of them.
In the 1958 session this house had passed a bill, No. C-48, to amend the Income Tax Act. When that bill went to the other place the Senate introduced certain amendments. The issue before the house turned on a particular amendment. That amendment was not one that purported to state rates of taxation. It was an amendment to section 71 of

the act which raised the question whether so-called foreign investment corporations should or should not be continued with an open-ended clause, or whether steps should be taken to prevent the creation of more of such corporations with the privileged tax position which such corporations enjoyed. It was on that amendment, Mr. Speaker-an amendment, as I say, which did not purport to deal with a particular rate of taxation-* that this house took its stand.
When the matter came up on July 14 you, Mr. Speaker, raised the question of order under standing order 63 which I just now read. The matter stood over and came up for debate on July 18. At that time the house took its position by decision that I think can be regarded as unanimous. There was certainly no division in the house, and there was no contrary opinion expressed. The house stood on the ground that this amendment to the Income Tax Act affected a money bill and there was no power in the Senate, under the constitution, to amend a money bill. This was not a supply motion; this was not a bill relating to the appropriation of money; it was a bill to amend the Income Tax Act. So I say, Mr. Speaker, the case is completely on all fours with the case now under debate.
Again I remind the house that it was not a clause in the Income Tax Act which related expressly to the rates of taxation. It was a clause to determine whether section 71 should be permitted to have continuing effect in relation to foreign business corporations. The house took its stand on these matters. Reference was made to the position taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in other sessions. The Leader of the Opposition concurred in the position, this historic position on which the government took its stand, and the house asserted that the amendment introduced by the Senate could not be accepted because it infringed upon the prerogative of this house to deal with money bills, which are not open to amendment by the Senate.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I accordingly move:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this house disagrees with the amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, for the following reason:
The amendment infringes the sole and undoubted right of the Commons to impose taxation; it alters the application of taxes and interferes with the public revenue.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this motion has just been made available to us-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Before the hon. member proceeds I should place the motion before the house, and I shall do so unless any hon. member wishes to raise a technical objection.
Customs Tariff
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I might raise the point as to whether notice of this motion is required. I am raising the question solely for information and not to make objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the rule is that notice is not required where the house is not accepting the amendment. The point which you raised on July 14, 1959 was that if a particular amendment was proposed to be accepted, notice must be given, but as to an amendment that was being rejected, no notice was required. When the matter stood over until July 18 for hearing you raised the matter again, as reported at page 6402 of Hansard when you said:
Before the Leader of the Opposition speaks, may I say this. I take it that the Minister of Finance considers that the proposed amendment does not now infringe on standing order 63 by reason of the fact that the remaining amendment does not alter any of the conditions, etc., of the grants involved.
To that observation I replied:
Exactly so, Mr. Speaker.
So when the motion simply stands upon and reasserts the provisions made by the House of Commons, no notice is required. Notice would be required if the house were being asked to accept an amendment introduced by the Senate. I think the rule is quite clear in standing order 63, and I may say it has always been the practice of the house that notice has not been required in cases where the house is standing on its original enactment and is not accepting the amendment proposed by the Senate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the point with which the minister has been dealing, and which was raised by my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate, the minister states that the motion is one of rejection of the amendment and not acceptance, and therefore no notice is required. I just bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the fact that the motion is not simply one of rejection, but it indicates the reasons for that rejection. We are asked 

and I am not at the moment complaining about this-to debate this motion immediately, without notice. The motion includes certain reasons why the amendment should be rejected, and these reasons have just at this moment been brought to our attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will not need to be reminded that in cases where an amendment proposed by the Senate is rejected, it is the practice to send a message to the Senate and give the reasons for the rejection. This is the long standing practice of the house. There are many precedents.

Customs Tariff
That does not touch the question of order that has been raised. That is to be determined on the question of whether or not the original enactment of the house is to stand. The position taken in this motion is that the enactment of the house should stand and the amendment should be rejected.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On the question of the necessity for notice, standing order 41, which applies to bills, etc., reads as follows:
Forty eight hours' notice shall be given of a motion for leave to present a bill, resolution or address, for the appointment of any committee, or for placing a question on the order paper; but this rule shall not apply to bills after their introduction, or to private bills-
And so on.
Notice has in effect been given to the house by the item being placed on the order paper under government orders, where it has stood for some time. It is, today, item 4, reading as follows:
June 15-Consideration of the amendment made by the Senate to Bill C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff-The Minister of Finance.
Note: Text of amendment printed in Votes and Proceedings of June 15 at page 671.
That is in effect the ordering of the consideration of this matter and it is open to the house, of course, to proceed in at least two directions. The item before the house is consideration of the amendment. This motion proposes to reject the amendment. Had the motion been to accept the amendment I might have been in the same position as I was in 1958, and would have had to bring to the attention of the minister that acceptance of the amendment would be contrary to standing order No. 63 and that, therefore, notice of the suspension of that standing order would have to be given. However, as the contrary course is suggested it would seem to me that notice and suspension of standing order 63 is not needed.
I am a little concerned about the motion in that it asks the house to disagree with the amendment rather than to reject it as being beyond the competence of the Senate, but that is made clear by the latter part of the motion, and I think I should place the matter before the house.

Before the point of order is left, I wonder if we might have some clarification of one part of Your Honour's remarks. I understood you to indicate that if a certain procedure had been adopted today, if a certain action had been taken, you would have had to indicate that rule 63 was applicable. Do I understand from this that Your Honour is making a finding that this proposed amendment by the Senate is in

fact in contravention of rule 63? It seems to me that this point has not been adequately dealt with.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not intend that to be a necessary implication of my ruling on the question of whether notice was needed. I did indicate that if the motion had been to accept the amendment then I would have had to consider that standing order 63 might be applicable and, therefore, would have to be suspended before the house, in accordance with its own rules, could properly proceed to discuss that proposition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We had expected, of course, that this morning we would be discussing a bill which in due course would be referred to the Senate, a bill of great and immediate urgency, so we had been told. However, instead we are at this moment discussing an amendment to a commons bill which has been received from the Senate. As you have pointed out, Mr. Speaker, this matter has been on the order paper for some time.
We should be perfectly clear about the nature of this amendment. The bill itself, to which the amendment has been made by the Senate, is of course a money bill, and it received long and careful consideration in this house. In the course of that consideration we in the opposition did our best to persuade the government not to take away the right of appeal against the decision of a single minister and the officials of the department of that minister in respect to important matters. That question was decided by the House of Commons in favour of the position taken by the government that provision for appeal should be removed. The bill was then sent to the other place.
The Senate has passed the bill with the amendment before us which has nothing to do with the substance of the measure, nothing to do with the financial or tax or monetary provisions of the bill, nothing to do with any revenue considerations which may be involved in the bill. The amendment made by the Senate is to restore the right of appeal from the decision of a minister by giving the person affected by that decision in respect to these important matters the right of appeal to the tariff board. That is the nature, that is the purpose, and that is the content of the amendment; it is designed to restore the right of appeal, a right which should never have been taken from the citizen by the House of Commons in this bill. This right of appeal is restored in the amendment by making it possible for a person against whom a decision has been made by the minister or by his department to appeal to the tariff board.

It has been said before, and it has been repeated by the Minister of Finance this morning, that this would mean inordinate delay and frustrate the working of the act. I would remind hon. members that this right of appeal is not to the tariff board and, through the tariff board, to the courts. That is the position which we took in this house when this matter was up for consideration. We felt that the full right of appeal should be retained, to the tariff board and to the courts. The hon. gentlemen in the other place, perhaps impressed by the argument that an appeal provision of that kind might result in undue delay, have restricted the right of appeal to the tariff board only. That is the only change they have made in this bill.
The minister told us this morning that this change is not acceptable to the government because the amendment which embodies the change is an unworkable one. Once again he told us that the right of appeal granted to a citizen from a decision of a minister means delay, and we cannot countenance delay; delay would make the act unworkable. Well, that is the excuse that is uttered by every governmental authority that wishes to take arbitrary power into its own hands. The minister says, in effect, we cannot have appeals because appeals mean delay and we cannot tolerate delay; we must act at once, by ministerial dictate if necessary.
The minister has said that this would mean exhaustive delay, and the reason it would be exhaustive is the fact that the tariff board is away behind in its work. He gave us some indication of the number of appeals which have been before the board and have not been decided after weeks and months. However, if the tariff board is in such a condition that it cannot deal with appeals of this kind with reasonable efficiency and expedition, then it is the responsibility of the government to see that it is strengthened so it can do just that.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is no excuse to say that the tariff board has been permitted, because of the multitude of duties which it now has, to get into a position where it cannot hear appeals in time so as to avoid affecting the procedure and operation of the act. There is no excuse for the government in that regard, particularly in view of the fact that it has done nothing for the board in an attempt to make it effective in the hearing of these appeals. The proper way to deal with this matter is to make it possible for the board to hear the appeals quickly and effectively, not by taking away the right of appeal. The Senate by its amendment merely restores
Customs Tariff
that right of appeal in a form which is less far-reaching and embracing than that which we on this side put forward when this bill was before the House of Commons earlier.
The minister has said a good deal about the constitutional implications of senatorial action in this matter. He has cited what are to him analogous precedents-they certainly are not analogous to us, and we will go into that matter later-to show that the Senate has no power to make this amendment. I seem to recall, though I have not all the details in mind, a couple of years ago the Senate making eight amendments to the estates tax bill, seven of which were accepted by the government when they came back to this house, yet at that time no suggestion was raised that it was unconstitutional for the Senate to make those changes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question. Does he not recall that the house was informed at that time that in accordance with long standing practice the Senate had been requested by the Minister of Finance on behalf of the government to make those particular amendments when the bill was before the Senate committee?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I recall that very well, but is the minister now trying to tell us that he has power over the Senate so that he can ask the Senate to do something which, if he had not asked it to do, would be unconstitutional?
That is what he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the Leader of the Opposition not agree that this has been the practice which has been carried on for many years by my predecessors? That is, when the government was prepared to accept an amendment the Minister of Finance asked the Senate committee to make the amendments, particularly in respect to matters usually not of far-reaching importance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It may be that has been the practice, but in the past I do not recall that the government of the day took exception to that kind of amendment by the Senate which did not deal directly with monetary provisions, such as that which the minister is saying now is unconstitutional. The minister may also remember-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are quite wrong.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister may remember that while he did suggest some of these amendments to the members of the other place, there was at least one which the government had not suggested nor approved at

Customs Tariff
the time, but accepted when it came back to the house. We can go into detail in this regard a little later.
The minister this morning has challenged the right ol the Senate to make an amendment to a bill which restores to Canadians the right of appeal from a decision of the minister. If that doctrine were established it would mean that no matter what provision was put in any kind of finance bill, even though it had nothing whatever to do with the financial clauses of the bill but a lot to do with other aspects, including rights of appeal, the Senate could never touch any portion of the bill dealing with such rights of citizens if the clause being amended was included in a money bill. That is the doctrine which the minister is trying to lay down in this House of Commons today.
So far as we are concerned, if the government wishes to alter beyond question the powers of the Senate in respect of this or any other matter, that is the government's responsibility. It will have a hard time proving that the Senate, in this particular case, does not have constitutional power to make this kind of an amendment, which is an amendment that does not directly concern any of these financial provisions but which is concerned exclusively with the right of appeal from a decision from the minister.
Mr. Speaker, if this amendment is not accepted by this house-and the government has made it quite clear that it is not going to be accepted-then presumably the house takes the stand that, having rejected the amendment, the bill is to be sent back to the Senate. I hope the normal and appropriate procedure will be followed in that case, and there will be a conference between the two houses in an effort to find a solution which safeguards the rights of the people by preserving the right of appeal in this case, but which will remove any legitimate objection the government could advance in respect to considerations of speed and efficiency of operation. That would be the normal course to follow if this amendment is rejected.
However, Mr. Speaker, so far as we are concerned we made our position very clear in regard to this matter when the bill was debated in the House of Commons earlier. We took the stand then that there should be an appeal and that the existing right of appeal should not be removed. We regret very much that it was necessary for the upper chamber to take steps to restore that right of appeal which had been removed by at least the majority of the representatives of the people in this house.

Mr. Speaker, I expect that the government is going to get its way in respect to this bill as it has in other matters, and I believe rightfully so. However, we are concerned as to the number of items in respect of which the government is beginning to get its way because of its obvious majority. I believe it was Lord Acton who said:
Power tends to corrupt; absolute power corrupts absolutely.
We have had a number of appropriate indications recently in this regard, and I need only refer to the debate which took place yesterday concerning the governor of the Bank of Canada. The original proposal of the government in this particular bill now before us was opposed by the opposition because in it we observed another indication of absolute power corrupting absolutely, in that the government was attempting to abolish the ordinary right of appeal to the tariff board.
I have always been of the opinion that one of the primary responsibilities of the other place as an institution is to ensure that no majority in this house is ever allowed to be used to the point where the rights of people, minorities and others in Canada, are abrogated arbitrarily.
I believe there is a very good reason outside of the obvious one why we are opposed to a minister of national revenue having final authority. A number of us in the opposition noted that a device which is proposed to give a minister complete and absolute authority might be used to raise tariffs by back door methods on the national scene. I believe the minister as much as admitted1 that when he spoke half an hour ago and indicated that the whole aim of the bill, which according to his contention is now being frustrated by the other place, was to enlarge job opportunities, employment opportunities in Canada. As the Conservatives of Canada have always used that term it has usually been allied with higher tariffs. It now becomes obvious that the reason the minister was to be given this arbitrary power was so he would have the right, as I said before by the back door method, to increase tariffs without Canadians really becoming aware that tariffs were in fact being increased.
I should like to endorse the proposal or contention of the leader of the official opposition. If the tariff board is so far behind in its work, our government is lacking in its responsibilities in that it does not ensure that the tariff board either is enlarged or other ways and means are discovered by which it can do its work with a little more dispatch than, in the words of the minister, it is now able to do.
The minister gave as an example of why he felt this amendment infringes the sole and

undoubted right of the commons to impose taxation. He went back to 1959 and said that example stands on all fours with the situation now before us. If I heard the minister correctly he informed us that in 1959 the other place was in fact attempting to tamper with the levels of revenue by seeing that certain corporations would not be able to take advantage of existing tax privileges.
I fail to see how the right of appeal stands on all fours with the right or otherwise of corporations to enjoy tax privileges. I hope before the debate ends the minister will look back into history, and if he does he may be able to come up with much sounder examples and precedents than the one he has given us.
The minister rather clearly underlined my basic contention when he admitted that the estate tax amendments were in a different category because in effect he, the minister, had asked the other place, according to his pronouncements today, to in fact exceed its authority and amend legislation having to do with the levels of revenue of the government.
I believe we shall have to continue to insist that the right of appeal to the tariff board, as proposed by the Senate, ought to be adopted by this house. I am glad that in this instance at least the Senate has performed a function which I had always been taught was one of the prime functions of the other place. Even though the government has a big majority in this house I hope if it really believes that the other place has any role to play at all-and there are many Canadians who are in doubt as to the validity of that proposition-then would it not agree that one of the prime reasons for the existence of the other place is to ensure that the basic rights of Canadians shall not be taken away from them by a majority in this house; and that therefore the other place is perfectly meeting at least one of its responsibilities when it attempts in this amendment offered to us to restore to Canadians the right of appeal which they have had over many long years.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps there is not very much one can add to what was said so well, so succinctly and so justly by the Leader of the Opposition. This is just another and an earlier example of what we have been witnessing in this house in recent weeks, the attempt of a government using, in the words of the Encyclopaedia Britannica in the article on the bill of attainder, a servile majority to establish a dictatorship in this country and to remove the individual citizen those very rights that the right hon. gentleman talked so much about only a year ago on this bill
Customs Tariff
of rights, about which he boasts so much and which he spends public money to circulate, with his own statements attached to it, for propaganda purposes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I think I should question the course the hon. member is taking as being outside the scope of the discussion. We are dealing with a specific amendment. References to the bill of rights and other extraneous matters ought not to be brought into the discussion unless they apply to this amendment. Bourinot deals with the matter in this way in the fourth edition at page 535:
When amendments made by one house to a bill from the other house are received back, and are under consideration-
This is our position this morning:
-it is not regular to discuss the bill itself, or its principle, or the policy of the government thereon; but the debate must be confined to the amendments.
Bascially the amendment is the insertion of the right of appeal. I do not want to circumscribe the discussion, but I wanted to put in that cautionary word before the hon. member got too far afield.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Surely this amendment, as you have just said, has to do with the restoration of the right of appeal which was taken away from the citizen as a result of the legislation passed in this house. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the effort on our part to restore the right of appeal has some relationship to the bill of rights where the right of appeal is supposed to hold.

I understand that Your Honour made no ruling but just issued a cautionary word which I thoroughly accept, because as hon. members will recall I made the argument in the house when the bill was before us before it was passed by this majority-I will not repeat the adjective I used, but I do think it applies in this instance-
But I will.

I have no doubt that my hon. and eloquent friend from Essex East will have something to say about this, and he far exceeds me in his capacity to describe this act of tyranny with adjectives which do not exist in my limited vocabulary, an act of tyranny that is all the more astonishing coming from the government headed by the author of the Canadian Bill of Rights, one part of which I now propose to read:
Every law of Canada shall, unless It Is expressly declared by an act of the parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the Canadian Bill of Rights, be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe or to authorize the abrogation, abridgment or infringement of any of the rights or freedoms herein recognized and declared, and in particular, no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to

(e) deprive a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations;
Now, sir why does parliament exist? Why did parliament come into existence in the first place? It came into existence to give the consent of the people to taxation and to avoid having taxes imposed by the crown or the minions of the crown, as every minister is. This is what these ministers seem to forget. They seem to think that because, under our system of responsible government, they have a majority behind them, parliament no longer matters; that they alone were chosen by the people and not all of us in this house. They think they were chosen by the people to speak for the people and to decide what the taxes should be and how they should be levied. This, sir, is not true, and the tyranny of the Queen's ministers can be just as great as the tyranny of the Queen before she had ministers sitting in parliament.
I say that what is being sought here, as we said when the bill was being debated before and as hon. ladies and gentlemen in another place have said-I might stop and say parenthetically that I congratulate the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. He must have found it rather difficult, and I respect him all the more, for having done it knowing the views that he and his party hold on the Senate, to pay the tribute he did to these ladies and gentlemen who seem to be more concerned about our liberties and our rights than the majority in this house. This is the issue, and the only issue. The suggestion, sir, that the method of determining the nature of articles to be assessed and the accuracy of the facts is an aid or a gift is a perversion of the English language such as perhaps only the Minister of Finance could do, as through his recent tactics he has demonstrated he is capable of doing.
I agree with that.

It seems to me that what is an aid or gift is the rate of duty, and the rate of duty is in no way affected by this matter. What is affected is the determination of the facts on which that duty shall be based and collected. It would be just as simple to say that the income tax that shall be paid will be whatever the minister of national revenue sees fit to exact from each individual Canadian; that is exactly parallel to what we are asked to do here. We are asked to say that the minister shall determine the conditions precedent, to use a phrase that is very dear to the Prime Minister, to the tax. The minister is to say of his own knowledge and in secret, because the facts are so secret- we know something about facts that are so 
secret, because we have learned something about them in the past few days-that they cannot be disclosed even to the tariff board.
This is what we were told by hon. gentlemen opposite during the course of the debate on this bill in this house. The taxpayer must not be allowed to know what the facts are on which he is being assessed; he has no right to know. The facts are so secret that they must be kept in the breast of the minister of national revenue, acting capriciously and beyond the right of appeal to any kind of tribunal.
This would have been serious enough if there had never been an appeal before, but there has been an appeal. This parliament over the years, and the Minister of Finance pointed this out in his presentation of the bill, has seen to it that the appeal was gradually strengthened. If I recall the circumstances correctly, and if I do not I would be very happy to be corrected by the minister, I think originally the appeal was from the customs officer who made the adjudication to a board which was merely an administrative board. This was not a very satisfactory form of appeal, but it was a form of appeal. Then Right Hon. R. B. Bennett set up the tariff board in its modern form, and there was an appeal to this tariff board which was a tribunal and court of record. From that time forward there has always been an appeal.
Now this house has decided, and is being asked to reaffirm the decision, that the right of appeal which less than a year ago was guaranteed by this parliament in the bill of rights, is to be taken away from the subject; that is the whole issue and the sole issue here. Why do hon. gentlemen want to do it? They do not tell us. They give the excuses, as the Leader of the Opposition has said, that every government seeking arbitrary power has always given; convenience, speed and secrecy. Dark deeds in dark places.
As a matter of fact, as I pointed out-and I was scoffed at by the treasury benches when I did so, but this was before certain revelations had been made in certain inquiries being held in other places-the Minister of National Revenue could make one adjudication for friends of the government and another adjudication for those who were not his friends. No reason would need to be given and there would be no access to any kind of information, no right of appeal to anyone. Not only do I say that could be done, but no one will believe that sooner or later, under some minister, it may not be done. I do not say it will be done; I am not saying any such thing, but I can remember speeches by the right hon. gentleman when he was sitting over here and did not have to account for his

words by his acts, when he could simply enunciate broad general principles without worrying at all about whether there was any conformity between his words and his deeds-
What are you doing now?

The hon. gentleman asks me what I am doing now. I am exercising one of the freedoms still left to us, the right of a freely elected member to speak in parliament. I notice an increasing number of the servile majority who think that right should be taken away from us, right in this chamber.
As I say, when the right hon. gentleman was sitting over on this side of the house, no one was more eloquent. He was far more eloquent, I think than anyone on this side of the house today, with perhaps one or two exceptions. I will not attempt to indicate who those exceptions are, except to say that I would not include myself. I, sir, am a plain man given to using plain language, to say yes when I mean yes and no when I mean no without resort to evasion or equivocation or dodging or squirming as hon. members opposite do. I say the right hon. gentleman, when he was over here, was always wont to point out, and about no one more than about me, that to give arbitrary power to ministers was the most dangerous thing that could possibly be done.
The right hon. gentleman made a promise in the election campaign. It was one of the many promises which he made and which are still just words. In the election of 1957 he promised that one of the first acts of the government of which he never expected to be the head would be to change the immigration regulations and the Immigration Act in order to deprive the minister of those arbitrary powers which he then had. Four years have passed and the only time that they attempted to change those regulations at all they were so laughed out of court that the hon. lady was obliged to come back and return to the regulations I had recommended to my colleagues. A promise in this regard has been made to amend the Immigration Act in every speech from the throne, but no change has been made.
The point I am making is this. If the minister of immigration should not have arbitrary powers-and it has been said by the right hon. gentleman that he should not have them-then considering the whole of English and Canadian constitutional history, and considering indeed the whole constitutional history of free countries, surely no minister should be given by any parliament the exclusive right to tax. Again to quote things that were often said by the right hon. gentleman when he was over here on this side of the chamber, the power to tax is the power to destroy;

and the power to tax in this particular measure is peculiarly the power to destroy.
What is the minister going to do? The minister is going to decide in one case that something could be made in Canada and thereby probably destroy the business of someone who wishes to import that article. In another case he is going to decide that it could not be made and thereby destroy the opportunity that some manufacturer might have of making it in Canada. The only criterion on which these decisions will be made will be the colour of the gentleman's eyes the size of his brief, or perhaps the size of something else.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen can fill in that third point for themselves. But having regard to the evidence we have as to how hon. gentlemen opposite have obtained some of the support they have obtained for themselves in recent elections, and having regard to some of the revelations that have been made in certain inquiries in the province of Quebec, I think the meaning of my words will be plain. I say that for us in this house to uphold the government in this attempt to restore to the crown the right to tax without the consent of the representatives of the people-a right that was taken away from the crown in the 14th century-is one of the most preposterous attempts at tyranny that we have ever witnessed.
Of course I do not think it was a conscious attempt at tyranny, but that makes it worse. Here is the Minister of Finance so oblivious of our history, so oblivious of our rights, so oblivious of all those things which are the foundations of our freedom that he comes in here and says that the convenience of this taxpayer or that taxpayer is more important than are the fundamental and immemorial of our rights, namely the right of the people through their representatives to consent to and control the taxes; and the right, moreover, of parliament-a right which has been very zealously guarded for over 100 years- to lay down precisely and surely the conditions upon which the subject will be taxed so that the tax exacted of one citizen will be on the same basis as the tax exacted of another citizen.
Under this bill there will not be the slightest assurance that such a thing will happen. In fact there will be absolute certainty that it will not happen. However wise the minister of national revenue may be-and I think the present minister is a great deal wiser than are most of his colleagues, but that is perhaps not saying a great deal-he is human and he is fallible. Out of his own wisdom, uncontrolled by any kind of inquiry, without

being under the obligation to give any kind of reasons for his decision, it is absolutely certain that he will not make the same decision on two sets of facts. From time to time it is certain to happen that a decision will be given one way in one case and another way in another case, even in good faith.
I do not impute to the hon. gentleman who temporarily has these functions any lack of good faith. I do not do that at all. That brings me to another point which is very important, which also was stressed very frequently by the right hon. gentleman opposite. It is not a matter of the person of the minister; it is not a matter of the character of the minister; it is a matter of the giving of power to any minister, however trustworthy. I do not think even the Prime Minister would insinuate that any less trustworthy minister ever sat in this house than my right hon. friend Mr. St. Laurent, yet the Prime Minister only yesterday made certain imputations-
The hon. member means "more trustworthy".

Everybody agrees.

I hope everybody will understand that is what I intended to say. I hope that no one will ever seek to denature that accidental slip of my tongue. Yet the Prime Minister pointed out quite truthfully yesterday that in 1945 Mr. St. Laurent himself recommended an order in council which was, as a matter of fact, kept secret; and it was kept secret for reasons that were considered by the government of the day to be good and sufficient, because the safety of the state was involved, as the right hon. gentleman knows and he knows what it was about. It is true that on one occasion in this house-and I never attempt to denature these facts-Mr. St. Laurent denied that there was any such order. He subsequently apologized to the house and explained something that I know is hard to credit; but knowing Mr. St. Laurent I am certain it was true. He explained that he had completely forgotten about the existence of the order.

speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Before we adjourned for the luncheon interval I made some reference to occasions in the past, some of them regrettable, when ministers held and sometimes exercised powers which it was necessary, though regrettable, to exercise in time of war. I had pointed out that those conditions were very different from normal conditions, normal taxing statutes in peacetime, as this present bill is. No one will pretend that this is a measure for the safety of the state.
There are sharp differences in the house about whether this bill is even good for the state, but that is not at issue, as Your Honour properly pointed out. We are not concerned now with whether or not this taxing statute in itself shall prevail, because it is going to prevail. We are concerned with whether or not, in the interpretation of this measure, the determination of what articles shall be taxable, and at what rates shall be done in the open with a right of appeal such as has existed for a long time, or whether that right shall, in defiance of the bill of rights, be taken away. That seems to be the sole issue here.

I do not think anyone in the country will be much impressed by hon. gentlemen arguing, as they are apt to argue whenever they have a weak case, that their predecessors may have done arbitrary things, or things which in their view were arbitrary, and that they therefore are at liberty to proceed in any way they please. I do not think such arguments would be effective, and for this reason; that they campaigned all across the country saying they were going to end that period of arbitrary rule and restore the rights of the people. I hope that neither the Prime Minister nor any of his colleagues will do what the Prime Minister seemed to be doing in another debate and suggest that because somebody else seemed to be doing something at some other time which, in his view, he was not justified in doing, the government is justified in doing wrong now.
That is the point. That is invariably the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite on occasions such as this. They seem to feel that the opposition in this house has no rights; no right to express an opinion because, they allege, at some time in the past, when some members of the present opposition were in office, it may have done some things which they felt were arbitrary. It seems to me that this kind of argument is only used by someone who has the weakest of weak cases. Yet I shall not be at all surprised if it is used again to provide another smokescreen, because that is the normal method by which this government evades, or seeks to evade, responsibility. It works for a while, but the public is gradually getting wise to it. This country is gradually realizing that the government is, in the first place, incapable of continuous and steady action of any kind and that it seeks, whenever things get out of hand, to find someone else to blame for its own incapacity.
But there is far more than incapacity involved here. This is a deliberate attempt to restore the ancient right which the crown claimed before parliamentary supremacy was established, the right to tax without the consent of the representatives of the people. Once that power is vested in a single minister, uncontrolled, unanswerable to the courts, as the government is seeking to do in this bill, the old control exercised by parliament will be gone. The government is seeking to go back to the days of ship money-

When I have finished. I am following the example of the hon. gentleman the other day, remembering the helpful intervention which he made on another occasion.

Hon. gentlemen opposite do not seem to like to hear the argument. I say that in the government's refusal to accept this amendment we have an attempt to turn back the clock-not the clock, because this goes back to the days before there were clocks-but an attempt to turn back the centuries to the days of the old feudal monarchs before the people had any say, before the people had any right to decide on the aids they would give to the crown. Under the guise of convenience, under the guise of safety, under the excuse that things must be kept secret, they say we must trust one minister, and he must not be questioned in what he does. We must trust him to decide what is taxable and at what rate, because by deciding what is taxable he is deciding at what rate it will be taxed.
Surely anyone who has any belief whatever in the rule of law, any belief whatever in the right of a subject to a fair hearing, any belief there should be no taxation without real representation, and any belief in the rights of parliament to make the tax laws in open parliament and not by the cabinet or a minister in secret, could not conceivably support the kind of legislation the government has advanced.

I do not intend to go into the past, but I did appreciate that fact coming from the hon. member because he had knowledge of what took place in the cabinet and was able to reveal it today. How it came about has been something we have been wondering about all through the years, and I know the historians of the future will pay their tribute to this historian for the contribution he has made today.

This is a taxation measure, and it being a taxation measure what are the rights involved? The Minister of Finance referred this morning to standing order 63 of the House of Commons, which reads in part:
All aids and supplies granted to Her Majesty by the parliament of Canada, are the sole gift of the House of Commons-
All through the years from the earliest times the Senate took the stand that it could make amendments, and it followed that course periodically and regularly. That was not the situation in the United Kingdom. We adopted in Canada a constitution similar in nature and kind to the British constitution. In the United Kingdom the position has been made very clear throughout the years, and was established centuries ago. The House of Commons has complete control of revenues and expenditures, and the House of Lords has no right to either initiate or amend money bills. Until about 1910 or 1911 the House of Lords did have the right to reject money bills, but that right was taken away by the parliament act of 1911. In the United Kingdom today money bills normally do receive the assent of the lords, but machinery is now available whereby money bills and other bills can become law without the concurrence of the House of Lords.
The hon. gentleman referred to antiquity and the foundations of parliament, and dealt at some length with parliamentary powers and prerogatives. It was on July 3, 1678, that the position of the commons and the lords was set out in a resolution of the house of commons of that day.
All aids and supplies granted to His Majesty in parliament are the sole gift of the commons, and all bills for the granting of any such aids and supplies ought to begin with the commons, and it is the undoubted right of the commons to direct, limit

and appoint in such bills the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants which ought not to be changed or altered by the House of Lords.

Mackenzie King and the manner in which he spoke of the Senate of his day, and I make no apology for referring to the Senate as such rather than the other place because I find that in the course of the arguments Mr. King advanced he invariably referred to that place as the Senate of Canada. I go back to July 19, 1924. As far as I am able to ascertain, this was the first time that Mr. King made any suggestion as to what he had in mind respecting the rights of the non-elected representatives of the people to thwart and interfere with, to amend, abrogate or otherwise alter the power of the House of Commons. Having in mind the action of the second chamber with respect to the measure which has just been amended and also the fate of a number of bills adopted by the commons and defeated in the Senate, I think hon. members will agree with me that the time has come when the commons in Canada should seek to gain rights and privileges with respect to legislation originating in this chamber similar to those which have obtained by the House of Commons in the parliament at Westminster. I may say that the government had under consideration, prior to the opening of this session, legislation with this end in view-
I stop to point out to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, the Boswell of Mr. Mackenzie King, that this was in 1924, and Mr. King had in mind at that time that something would be done. I refer to what he said:
The government had under consideration, prior to the opening of this session legislation, with this end in view, but we were anxious the public should feel fully convinced of the necessity before pressing it on the attention of parliament. 1 desire to assure the house that when parliament reassembles steps will be taken by the government to obtain, if possible, means whereby bills may be enacted by and with the advice and consent of the House of Commons under conditions similar in principle to those which have been sanctioned for the parliament of the United Kingdom.

He continued in power until 1926, and then for a short interval he was out of power. He returned to power. The Senate was going to be reformed. A little later on he told Canada quite candidly

how the reform came about, namely by substituting live Grits for dead Tories. That was the nature of the reformation. This went on, and then he entered into an arrangement whereby each of his appointees to the Senate was required to sign an undertaking as to what he would do after he got there.
Well, in 1947 Mr. King referred to the nature of those undertakings. I do not want to clutter up the record too much, but each and every one, as appointed to that body, was asked a question by Mr. King. He was asked for an assurance of support of such measure of Senate reform, in conformity with the requirements of the constitution, as might be introduced by the Liberal administration. He went on to say that this assurance had been given by all who had accepted appointment to the Senate within the time mentioned. Well, that was the last we ever heard about that subject, except in subsequent elections. Now we are in the position where the House of Commons of Canada has spoken. Whatever arguments are advanced today- and they were advanced before, and I am not here for the purpose of answering them- this legislation is taxation legislation. Again I thank the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate; I wish to repeat the thanks. I am sorry he did not continue in law, because after all he has given his opinion-based not only on his experience as a law student but also as a former clerk of the privy council and as a minister of the crown-that this is taxation legislation. He has made that clear. This house passed it. The purpose in mind was the provision of jobs and the assurance that unnecessary delay would not take place in regard to a matter which has to a considerable extent crippled the productive and industrial capacity of Canada. I refer to the bringing into Canada of goods of a class, or so close to a class or kind, manufactured in Canada so as to permit evasion of the legislation which exists for the preservation of Canadian jobs in Canadian industry.
I am glad to see hon. gentlemen opposite on the side they are on this matter. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, "we did this and that, but those were days when things were serious." If I were to believe what hon. gentlemen opposite have endeavoured to lead the Canadian people to believe, I would think we were living in one of the most serious economic days that Canada has ever seen.
That is true.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
They have been asking for action. Having listened just yesterday to the hon. member for Essex East, I wondered whether he could maintain silence. It is very difficult.

This is the most serious time in Canadian economic history.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I seem to remember another time that was fairly serious for the hon. member for Essex East, but I am not going into that now. I am pointing out this is a taxation measure. There were a few Liberals in the Senate who saw the situation as it was.

Subject only to an appeal to the tariff board-
That is the essential part of the amendment. Now, as to relevance; surely the argument must relate to the amendment. Surely it cannot go over the rather interesting field that the Prime Minister has been discussing, however interesting that may be for discussion on another occasion when other subjects are before the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: May I simply suggest that possibly the hon. gentleman was not here when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate dealt with the subject.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I think it would be helpful to get your guidance as to whether, on this particular amendment from the Senate, we can discuss the main bill and whether we can discuss the reform of the Senate and the powers of the Senate.

Perhaps if I read the motion before the house it will help to answer the question which has been raised in the point of order, namely the relevance of what has been said about the Senate. by the Senate to Bill No. C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, for the following reasons: The amendment infringes the sole and undoubted rights of the commons to impose taxation; it alters the application of taxes, and interferes with public revenues.
