speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I had arrived, when I was given a rest by reason of an interruption that had no basis, at the point of saying that the House of Commons dealt with all the arguments. Hon. gentlemen expressed themselves strongly. They talked for nine days. This reminds me also of the fact that the hon. gentleman who just finished speaking said we were getting to the point where they could not express themselves. Yet we had nine days of talk. There was a careful examination, very helpful and beneficial.
I can also say to the hon. gentleman that the newly found reformation on his part is welcome after the way in which freedom was crucified in this house by the closure imposed when those four hon. gentlemen over there were members of the government. I have made an error, Mr. Speaker; I included the hon. member for Laurier, who was absent at that time in better climes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It would not be the first error you have made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I pointed out the fact that this bill was discussed and went over to the other place. A few members of the other place saw otherwise, but they decided that they were going to amend a taxation bill. Let me make this clear. We are not going to accept their amendment of this taxation bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Down with the right of appeal.
To hell with the bill of rights.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
They have all got the
same refrain, Mr. Speaker; the bill of rights. The thing they ridiculed they now found all their arguments upon.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, you have torn it up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
I do not want to enter into conflict with them, I simply want to state the facts. Their leader in the Senate chose to immediately give an indication of what would be done. I say this, and I repeat it; that the question as to whether or not the Senate of Canada is going beyond that responsibility which it has discharged and can discharge with effectiveness under the

constitution is a question that the Canadian people will have to decide sooner or later.
We will meet you halfway.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
I notice that in response to that remark there was but one lone voice over there, and he used the top of his desk. Otherwise there was silence at that moment.
The other place has over and over again in the past four years made amendments that have been beneficial and helpful in the discharge of its joint legislative responsibility. The bills have come back here amended and we have accepted them. On one occasion, at least, the amendments were very close to the line, if not over the line. We made it clear there was no precedent being created thereby.
In this case this government takes its stand. We shall not, as the Minister of Finance has said, accept the authority or right of the Senate to make this amendment. I hope the house will agree with that stand. The bill will be sent back to that body. If they choose to stand on what they have done this legislation, beneficial to the Canadian people, legislation that has universally been requested, can only pass out of existence, for we on our side will not accept the amendment. In the days ahead we shall ascertain the constitutional rights of this country in the only way in which they can be ascertained.
I said a moment ago that that would be sooner or later. I remember so well another occasion when the challenges were given as to what was going to happen-"and soon"- so I say this. This is a major matter. It was discussed in detail for nine days. Whatever the demerits, every argument that could be advanced was advanced by the opposition, strongly and fearlessly. This house, if we are to maintain the Canadian constitution, cannot in taxation matters be subject to the untoward interruption and interference of the other house. I make that clear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister a question. Is the position he takes that the government refuses to accept the restoration of the right of appeal from a decision of the minister, and is willing to stand or fall on that issue?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, even the Leader of the Opposition should understand clearly what I have said. There was none of that equivocation, and fence straddling, for which he has become famous.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister now answer my question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: It is answered.
Mr. Speaker, unlike the Prime Minister, I shall endeavour to address myself to the question before the house.
Oh, oh.

I admit at once, of course, that I do not have the skill of the Prime Minister in the art of irrelevance and trying to throw up a smokescreen so as to mislead anyone who will read his remarks. If I had that skill, Mr. Speaker, I assure you that I should not desire so to use it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: You are safe.
The interjection of the Minister of Public Works was one that I did not hear. Perhaps it is just as well that I did not hear it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Do you want to hear it?

I should not like to have to answer my old classmate and colleague in the way in which he should be answered and dealt with.
The business before the house is consideration of the amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff. As is indicated on the order paper, the amendment of the Senate is contained in June 15 Votes and Proceedings at page 671. I should like to read it in order to make my point. It goes on to say:
A message was received from the Senate informing this house that the Senate had passed Bill C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, with the following amendment:-
Page 1. lines 22 and 23: Strike out lines 22 and 23 and substitute therefor the following:
"(3) Subject only to an appeal to the tariff board, the decision of which board shall be final and in respect of which appeal the provisions of section 44 of the Customs Act shall apply mutatis mutandis, the minister shall decide the following matters: ",
It will be noted that the only significant change in that amendment is with reference to the right of appeal from the minister. The minister's power to decide is left unhampered.
The Minister of Finance this morning in dealing with this matter, when he set it out, indicated to the house that he proposed to reject the amendment of the Senate. It is quite the privilege of the house, if it wishes to do so, at any time to reject a proposed amendment of the Senate. But he went on to say this, and I think this motion should be read again to the house because it completely ignores any relationship to the amendment before us. As I said earlier, the Prime Minister seemed to me to completely ignore the whole matter before the house in an effort to find an issue where he could drag up, for some purpose of his own, the question of
Customs Tariff
Senate reform. That is a subject that I might be very interested in discussing on a proper occasion. The motion now before the house, without notice, by the Minister of Finance is the following:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this house disagrees with the amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, for the following reason:
The amendment infringes the sole and undoubted right of the Commons to impose taxation; it alters the application of taxes and interferes with the public revenue.
It is elementary, of course, that the Senate have no right at all, or that the House of Commons has the sole and undoubted right, to impose taxation. That is elementary. I do not know why that reference is put in this motion before us now. It is irrelevant. I perhaps should have pressed the point harder earlier when Your Honour was putting the question, but it seems to me that it has no relationship to the business before the house at all and that that part of the amendment is irrelevant to the subject matter before the house. If such commentary is permitted in a motion rejecting an amendment of this sort, the one before us dealing with the right of appeal, then of course we could add any other commentary. We might add some facetious commentary such as, for instance, that we did not like the names of the hon. senators or any other comments we wished to add. Neither the minister nor the Prime Minister made any attempt whatever to relate that part of the motion to the amendment proposed by the Senate. They glossed it over and talked about Senate reform and other matters that are not before us on this occasion.
The Minister of Finance did the house a real disservice in his argument when he made reference to the income tax amendments proposed by the Senate in 1959. As I recall it the situation was this. Since I did not know the line which the Minister of Finance was going to take in dealing with this Senate amendment I have not looked the matter up, but I think my recollection of it is correct. The house had proposed a change in section 71 of the Income Tax Act closing the class of companies that could be called foreign corporations, formerly called 4-K companies. I believe that was the terminology. The significance of that was that no companies incorporated in the future would do other than pay income tax or corporation tax in the ordinary way. That type of corporation with which we were concerned on that occasion, namely the foreign corporations, paid only a nominal type of tax. I think it was $100, but I am subject to correction as to the amount.

That is right.

Customs Tariff
In any event, the house dealt with that taxation matter. The Senate proposed an amendment striking out that part of the provision in the amending bill.
The whole clause.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member for Ottawa West will allow me to interrupt him. There is a good deal of conversation going on, and I think a good deal of it comes from the corridor. If hon. members cannot moderate their voices I suggest that they go into the lobby, as it is very difficult to hear what is being said.

The Senate amendment on that occasion struck out the clause in the bill, and the effect of it was virtually to exempt from corporation taxation all companies of the type which 1 have described or which might be incorporated in the future.
And it changed the revenue.

In other words it related to the imposition of taxation on the companies with which we were concerned on that occasion, and there was no question at all but that they were seeking directly to undo the imposition of taxation imposed by this House of Commons. There can be no question in the mind of anyone so far as I know that they had no right to do that. Certainly I am not aware that anyone in this House of Commons suggested that they had the right to pass such a clause.
The matter before us today has no such connotation at all. It is a very narrow point. What the Senate chose to do is this. Although from reading the debates I believe that some of them did not like the legislation, they chose to accept any parts of the legislation that had any implications of taxation at all. They completely ignored that point, and they dealt only with the right of the taxpayer to be heard by way of appeal from the arbitrary decision of the minister. The essential part of the amendment is in adding the words:
Subject only to an appeal to the tariff board,-
They dealt with that one matter, and that alone. I ask the house-
In open court.

-where that infringes or has any relationship to taxation. Where does it deal with taxation? This resolution with which the house is now dealing goes on to give reasons for rejecting the amendment:
The amendment infringes the sole and undoubted right of the commons to impose taxation-
Is the Minister of Finance suggesting for one moment that an appeal to the tariff board from an arbitrary finding of a minister is

imposing taxation? If he is, then he is suggesting-and this is implicit in his argument- that the minister concerned in making that decision acted not in accordance with the law and the definitions spelled out in a statute, but that he broke the law and did something under his arbitrary powers that was not in accordance with the statute.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the issue.

Then the minister asks us to reject the Senate amendment for the following additional reason:
-it alters the application of taxes-
The application of taxes is clearly set out in the bill and in the act; every detail of the application of taxes is set out there. The Senate has not dealt with any aspect of the bill relating to the application of taxes. The only conclusion that can be drawn from the minister's motion is that the minister is suggesting that an appeal to the tariff board deciding what the law was in its application might show that the minister had broken the law and the tariff board had brought him back; that the appeal authority under the provisions of the act was altering the application of taxes. Surely the minister is not going to ask this house to believe that the whole purport of this legislation, the whole purport of giving this final right of decision to the minister was so that the minister could act arbitrarily outside the legislation. Yet that is what his motion means.
Then the minister argued that taking an appeal from the minister's decision to the tariff board would interfere with the public revenue. If the tariff board decision upheld the minister it would be difficult to see how the right of appeal would interfere with the revenue. But if the tariff board overruled the minister because the minister had made a wrong finding in fact, or had misapplied1 the law, would that be interfering with the public revenue, or would that be interfering with a wrongful action taken by a minister contrary to the law enacted by this House of Commons? That is the point at issue here. In other words, the minister's reasons as given in the motion which is before us are completely specious and irrelevant to the rejection of the amendment to this bill received from the Senate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Another smokescreen.

It is a complete non sequitur
and is not to be related to the Senate amendment at all.
Just to hide the Coyne issue.

My seatmate gives a good reason as to why it was done. I would perhaps

be called to order, Mr. Speaker, if I were to elaborate on why it was done. It is obviously done to divert the attention of the House of Commons from the real issue.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear; for no other reason.

The real reason for the motion before us is whether the Senate amendment giving a right of appeal to the tariff board from the minister's arbitrary decision will be accepted or rejected by this house. That is the real issue.
To divert attention from the Coyne affair.

This attempt to drag in all these extraneous matters is one that I am afraid has been used all too often these days by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. Perhaps I had better not enter into the debate of yesterday, when we saw the Minister of Finance struggling hard1 for what many of us thought were diversionary tactics.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He thinks he has got a reprieve.
In answer to this point-
The fishing is not any better.

In regard to the matter before the house today the Prime Minister chose-and I regret that he has left the house now, because I would have liked him to be here when I deal with this-to deal with an order in council passed just at the conclusion of the last great war, at a time when this country had many hundreds of thousands of troops in other parts of the world. We were looking forward to bringing them back here. They had fought a very long, hard war. I need1 not remind hon. members of this house about that; a great many hon. members are familiar with that in a personal way.
That order in council was dragged into this debate today by the Prime Minister as a red herring. That order in council which was passed related to a matter of the security of this nation having to do with a world spy ring having been discovered, and an urgent attempt being made to deal with that situation. The issue was whether or not the war was over; whether we were immediately likely to be engaged in another war. That matter concerned our whole security.
Just before I came into the chamber at 11 o'clock this morning I had delivered to my office the text of the speech which the Prime Minister made only the day before yesterday-

To the Kiwanis clubs.

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the rule that my learned friend has just invoked as to what is in order and what is not, is he not at the moment hoist on his own petard? This is completely irrelevant.

speechtext: Why doesn't my hon. friend from Essex East sometimes speak with even a kernel of truth?

speechtext: He has never dug a ditch in his life.

speechtext: I shall keep in mind the point of order as the hon. member proceeds.

Mr. Speaker, I thought the Minister of Public Works was not in the chamber when the Prime Minister was dealing with this order in council. I merely want to contain my remarks within the limits of the point raised by the Prime Minister, who raised this matter in some illogical way that I could not understand as a reason for rejecting this amendment from the Senate. I could not see the relevance of the two. I did not understand what that 1945 order in council about which the Prime Minister spoke had to do with the right of appeal to the tariff board and the arbitrary decision of the minister. The Prime Minister was permitted to make reference to it and I thought I should be permitted the same latitude in replying to the argument he raised in regard to that order in council.
The Prime Minister was regrettably very careful not to give the house the subject matter with which that order in council was concerned or the situation in which the house found itself at that time. As hon. members who were here in those years will recall, the War Measures Act had regrettably to be used during the five years from 1940 to 1945. I think it was not other than distasteful to hon. members that the circumstances at the time made that practice necessary, but the point I was seeking to make was the complete

Customs Tariff
irrelevance of the Prime Minister's attempt to relate that order in council to the question which is before us. The matter of the reform of the Senate is also, of course, completely irrelevant to the point before us now. The message from the Senate contains a simple amendment having to do with the right of a citizen or, perhaps I should more correctly say, a taxpayer, to appeal to an administrative board which has grown up over the years and the authority of which has been so extended that it is now a court of record. It has to do with the taxpayer's right to an assurance that the taxation law as applied to him will be applied in accordance with the statutes of this land. That is all this amendment contains-nothing more, and nothing less.
The Prime Minister would have us believe there is some greater justice in having the taxation law of the land applied by the minister alone without right of appeal and without his being obliged to give any reasons for the decisions he takes in cases of this type where matters of fact have to be determined. The Minister of Finance, in the course of remarks which were singularly brief for him, went on to give as the reason for the position taken by the government the greater speed and efficiency which would result. In the argument which he addressed to this point the hon. gentleman used language which was identical with the language used in this country in the late 1930's by those persons who were apologizing for the fascist regime in Italy. I could not help but recall how many times some people in this country-fortunately, a minority, not a majority-used as an apology for that regime of that day the fact that they got the trains running on time. That was the theme of the small part of the argument put forward by the Minister of Finance which was relevant this morning, the only real reason he gave for not wanting taxpayers to have the right of appeal to the tariff board.
The Prime Minister, in his concluding remarks, seemed to adopt and approve this argument used by the Minister of Finance, as indeed, I would expect him to have done, but I point out to the Prime Minister that mere efficiency or ease of administration is not the test when you are applying onerous taxation to the citizens of this country. Surely something better than that should be the test.
For my part, I must say it is a matter of regret that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) is not with us today. I wish to express my personal regret at his illness and his absence. I wish he were here, and I hope his colleagues will convey my regrets to him. I, for one, have never been convinced in the course of this legislation that the Minister of

National Revenue knew that this provision was in the bill in the first instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh. He stood up in this house and supported it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Surely the hon. member does not believe that.

Well, I can speak for myself. The hon. member for Edmonton West can interject as much as he wishes and speak as much as he wishes. I shall always protect his right to speak. I have that feeling in any event. I believe that had the cabinet had the benefit of the advice of the Minister of National Revenue on this measure since it has come back from the Senate the message we would now be sending back to the Senate would be one of concurrence in the proposed amendment. That is my assessment of the man and, as I say, I regret he has unfortunately been ill, and unable to give the benefit of his views to the cabinet on this point since it was dealt with by the Senate.
I know the Minister of Finance has a somewhat different outlook on these things. Once he has put a provision in a bill, good bad or indifferent, he will stand by it no matter how wrong it is shown to be in the course of debates in this house or by an amendment from the other place. I regret that the minister takes this attitude. I regret, also, that the Prime Minister in seeking to deal with the issue before us at this time chose to deal with many side issues which are interesting and, indeed, important, but which are irrelevant to this particular motion. The rest of the right hon. gentleman's arguments had mainly to do with personalities. I have sought in my observations to steer clear of personalities and to relate my remarks directly to the point of issue. I, for my part, must support the right of the taxpayers of this country to appeal from the arbitrary decision of the minister to the tariff board. This was a right which they had enjoyed. It was taken away by this House of Commons, and I wish to see it restored to them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
am sure everyone in this house appreciates the kind reference which the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) has made to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). We all regret that he is not here today. I think that if he were here he would give an answer to the observation which the hon. member for Ottawa West made about his attitude in regard to this bill. I think the hon. member has misrepresented the opinion which the Minister of National Revenue would have expressed on this matter.

The hon. member for Ottawa West seems unable to appreciate the nature of the legislation which is before us. He has regarded this as a very simple matter. All we have here, he says, is a simple amendment which is going to protect the interests of the taxpayers. Well, who are the representatives of the taxpayers of this country? Are we not their representatives? Have we not been elected as members of this house to be their representatives? Any decision which is made here is made in the interest of the taxpayers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You would not think so.

The hon.
member has said that this is simply an amendment granting a right of appeal to the tariff board. But the hon. member has chosen to overlook a rule of this house which was established when Canada became a nation in 1867. I am referring to standing order 63 which was read by Your Honour:
All aids and supplies granted to Her Majesty by the parliament of Canada, are the sole gift of the House of Commons, and all bills for granting such aids and supplies ought to begin with the house, as it is the undoubted right of the house to direct, limit, and appoint in all such bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which are not alterable by the Senate.
Is this present bill, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, a bill which grants aid and supply to Her Majesty? Anyone who listened to the historical references in the speech of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) would certainly have thought that this was a bill to grant aid and supply to Her Majesty, because he spoke of the arbitrary power which was given to the minister to collect taxes and to alter taxes.

Would the minister permit a question arising out of his reference to standing order 63? Does he suggest that the Senate amendment respecting the right of appeal to the tariff board is related to such grants as are the subject of standing order 63, or is an aid or supply within the meaning of standing order 63?
I think anyone with a fair mind reading standing order 63 which I will read again for the hon. member-
I have it before me.

The hon. member says he has it there; perhaps he would look at it. It reads:
All aids and supplies granted to Her Majesty by the parliament of Canada, are the sole gift of the House of Commons-
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I have to go into detail to explain for the benefit of the

hon. member the meaning of the words "sole gift of the House of Commons".
That is elementary.

Standing order 63 then continues as follows:
-and all bills for granting such aids and supplies ought to begin with the house-
This bill began with the house. The standing order then continues:
-as it is the undoubted right of the house to direct, limit, and appoint in all such bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions-
What is the condition here? The condition here is that it shall be decided by the minister, whose decision shall be final.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Hon. members opposite do not agree with me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the way all tyrants begin.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You should know.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
What meaning does the Leader of the Opposition ascribe to the words "limitations and qualifications of such grants which are not alterable by the Senate"? If they are not alterable by the Senate then the Senate has no power to alter them. Has the Senate altered them in this instance? Yes; for we have before us today an amendment which is in essence an alteration of the bill granting aids and supplies to Her Majesty. No one can question the fact that a bill dealing with customs tariffs is a bill granting aids and supplies to Her Majesty.
The hon. member for Ottawa West is probably as familiar as anyone in this house with the fact that the Customs Tariff involves hundreds of items and deals practically entirely with the collection of taxes through customs and exise and by other means. Therefore, the amendment to this bill is precisely that which is not allowable because this is a bill which is not alterable by the Senate.
The question which we are concerned with is not merely a question of whether a right is being refused to taxpayers to prevent them from appealing a decision of the minister to the tariff board but is a question as to whether we are going to acquiesce in an amendment by the other place which it has no right to make. That is the real question before us today.
If the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Ottawa West think that this is a bill dealing with taxation, and I believe they are right, they must also agree that it is unalterable by the Senate. The hon. member for Ottawa West believes

Customs Tariff
that it is a taxation bill because, to use his own words as I wrote them down-
I think perhaps I can help the minister. The point I made was that the bill in toto is not before us but only the amendment dealing with the right of appeal.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I beg your pardon?
I suggested that it was only the amendment to the bill that was before us and argued that the whole bill was not now before us.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon.
member also stated that this was something affecting the taxpayers. I suggest if it affects the taxpayers it does so in respect to a matter of taxation; that is, taxes they must pay. I think the hon. member will agree with that, because if there is any complaint on the part of taxpayers it has to do with the taxes which they must pay being unfair and they, therefore, want to appeal to the tariff board to make it right. That being correct, there is no doubt, using the hon. member's own argument, that this bill deals with taxation. I think it is unnecessary for me to argue any further along that line.
To reinforce my suggestion that this is not unusual, I point out that there are hundreds of provisions in public statutes granting to ministers discretionary powers more or less of this type.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was the minister for citizenship and immigration for three or four years and I am sure that no one knows better than he the discretionary powers he possessed while acting in that capacity. The hon. member for Ottawa West, who was the parliamentary assistant to the minister of defence production, knows full well the powers that the minister of defence production possesses. Who in this country has ever possessed greater powers than the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe?
Are you arguing against that?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, no, the
hon. member does not follow my argument.
Oh, yes, I do.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I should like to point out-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not even an argument.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) says this is not even an argument, the fact that many ministers have discretionary powers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was referring to youi speech as a whole as not being even an argument.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose when the hon. member for Laurier was the minister of transport he had many powers which he could exercise and did exercise without there being granted any right of appeal from his decisions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not know of any.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Now-lan) under the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff Act has many other powers apart from this one given by this bill from which there is no appeal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: There are 64.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Revenue that there are 64 different powers which have been in existence from which there is no appeal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Is the logic of his argument that whenever possible we should reduce and take away these rights of appeal just because there are 64 instances which exist where there is no right of appeal?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, that is not my argument.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, what is your argument.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am trying to point out some of the inconsistencies in the arguments presented by hon. members of the official opposition. I am attempting to show that we are not doing something quite original and out of keeping with the history of this country as has been suggested by those hon. members. No one knows better than those hon. gentlemen who were members of the previous ministry, that these powers have existed, because some of them and their colleagues exercised these powers when they held office.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is that your excuse?

No, sir. The Leader of the Opposition knows very well that no one would attempt to alter all the powers and discretions that are given to various ministers, some of which are very necessary for the administration of the country. That is the reason this amendment was put into the Customs Tariff. That is, it is considered necessary at this time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But the right of appeal existed for years.
The House of Commons saw fit to pass this bill and the members of the other place felt they had the power to alter it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, the power to put back the right of appeal.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The House of Commons is now being asked whether the other place has the right to alter it and whether this house is going to maintain the rights and privileges, as well as duties, established as part of the constitution of this House of Commons and, therefore, of this country, in 1867 as contained in standing order 63.

Mr. Speaker, I rise because I feel that the Solicitor General (Mr. Browne), and I am sure not intentionally, misrepresented what I said. I have the words I actually used and feel that 1 should be permitted under the rules to set the record straight.
The Solicitor General gave the impression that I suggested that the amendment we are now considering was in itself a taxing statute. What I said was that this whole bill was a normal taxing statute. I continued, and these are the precise words I used, to say that there are sharp differences in the house about whether this bill is even good for the state, but that is not at issue, as Your Honour properly pointed out. We are not concerned now with whether or not this taxing statute in itself shall prevail because it is going to prevail. We are concerned with whether or not, in the interpretation of this measure, the determination of what articles shall be taxable, and at what rates, shall be done in the open with a right of appeal such as has existed for a long time, or whether that right shall, in defiance of the bill of rights, be taken away. That seems to be the sole issue here.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to indulge in any technical or legal hairsplitting on this issue. We in this group simply oppose this issue on the basis of what is in the best interest of the people. I am a simple country man searching for the truth in the dense political fog which has been created by repeated government errors in recent days. I rise to express our opposition to this very unique and, I would say, unusual resolution, and to express our concern over the unreasonable things that have occurred in recent days.
Customs Tariff
The second paragraph of this resolution simply diverts attention from the principle of an appeal on, from our point of view, a very trivial basis indeed.
I listened with interest, as I always do, to the orchidaceous rhetoric of the Prime Minister and the speech delivered in such a dramatic manner which made us all feel as though there was a crisis in it. Anyway, it was obvious from the Prime Minister's remarks that he has clearly indicated he refuses to accept the amendment proposed by the Senate that restores the right of appeal to the Canadian people from the decision of a minister or of officials. We think that right of appeal is fundamental. It has been mentioned on a number of occasions by the spokesmen of the official opposition and by the members of this group. In our opinion on this occasion the Senate has performed a service for the Canadian people. Hon. gentlemen of the other place have protected the rights of the Canadian people in, shall I say, taking this second look and finding out the weaknesses in the legislation that was sent over to their house. That legislation received a great deal of attention in this house. Fears were expressed during the rather lengthy and at times heated debate that this was a wrong principle to establish in legislation and the Senate has vindicated that opinion as expressed by a good number of members of the opposition during that debate.
I judge from the Prime Minister's remarks that he challenges the house to oppose his will. This is the way I take it. From the very emphasis he used and the dramatic way in which he brought the matter to the attention of the house there was no question but that he challenges the house to oppose him. I did not sense in his speech the question of a great principle. The Prime Minister challenged the house to oppose his will. You could see all the power vested in the Prime Minister and all the determination of one self-willed man to impose his will on this House of Commons. Members of this group accept this challenge and welcome an immediate appeal to the highest court of the land, which is the people.
Let's go home and settle this problem.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The election is not going to be held today.

I am distinctly under that impression, Mr. Speaker, and possibly not next month. The Prime Minister blows this thing up as a great issue. You could see in his attitude and in his remarks that he thought to himself, now, I have got something that

Customs Tariff
will befog the minds of the Canadian people. This is an issue; this is a smokescreen; this is something I can take pleasure in presenting. I can see him rampaging around the country talking about the members of the opposition disregarding the rights of parliament.
True.

We must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that no one was more vociferous in days past with respect to reform of the Senate and no one has said less since he was elected to office with respect to the suggested reform of the Senate than the Prime Minister. This is not a major issue. What are the issues in this country if the government should go to the country?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I hope the hon. member is not going to answer his own question because it would be out of order.
I am using a counter-argument as against this being the issue. In doing so I think I must propose what are the issues.
Let us keep on one side of the case.

The issues are not this one. The issues are unemployment, markets, health insurance, security and justice for old persons. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister wishes to go to the country at this time the Canadian people will not be misled by the presentation of what is obviously an expedient, a manufactured and synthetic issue. Therefore we on this side of the house, say, let the people decide now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker,-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must inform the house if the minister speaks now he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate has exemplified on the part of the opposition some quite extraordinary features but they are quite obvious, and I shall not detain the house long in speaking of them.
Hon. members must have been conscious of a curdling of their blood here today, Mr. Speaker, as they listened to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate tell them that the day of freedom had passed and we are now under the rule of tyranny. The hon. member for Kootenay West was just talking about blowing something up into a great issue. If there was any blowing up done in this house it was done by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in what he had to say about the effects of this measure. He was talking about the danger of the bill in question if passed, without the benefit of the amendment introduced by the Senate. This house has

dealt with this matter, Mr. Speaker. It was before the house on nine different days of the present session. On April 18 the house gave this bill second reading without amendment by a vote of 141 to 34, and on April 19 the measure was passed on third reading on division, a division not called by the Liberals but by the hon. member for Assiniboia. He called out "on division" and that is the only record there is of a division of opinion in the house on the third reading of the bill.
But the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate curdled our blood by talking about "dark deeds in dark places". Well, I think his following comments indicated that probably he knew more about the subject of dark deeds in dark places than any other member of this house. What are those dark deeds which he fears, Mr. Speaker, as a result of the enactment of this measure without the Senate amendment? Without traversing ground that is already so familiar, may I say that this measure simply follows well established precedents in this house. Hon. members opposite were not lying awake at nights as they dreamed about the loss of freedom when they were in power. Is freedom passing in the United Kingdom?
It is passing here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is tyranny overcoming freedom there, Mr. Speaker? I have already drawn to the attention of the house that under similar legislation of the United Kingdom power is given to the treasury in just such cases without any right of appeal. Here are the notes issued by the board of trade and commissioners of customs and excise under the Import Duties Act. This is the official note:
Under the Import Duties Act, 1958, protective duties are normally chargeable on imported machinery in order to protect United Kingdom machinery manufacturers.
And then they say this about duty free admission:
Section 6 of the 1958 act and paragraph 1(b) of the fourth schedule thereto provide that the treasury may, on the recommendation of the hoard of trade, direct that payment shall not be required of any duty chargeable under section 1 of the 1958 act on particular importations of machinery,-
Some exceptions are set out and then the following words appear:
-if similar articles are not for the time being procurable in the United Kingdom.
The decision in that matter is not subject to appeal. It is a decision made by the treasury.
Further on in this document, Mr. Speaker, we find the following:
The similarity of machines for the purposes of compliance with the statutory condition referred to in paragraph 1(b) is judged primarily in relation

to the product or effect and the efficiency with which it is produced. The appearance, size, shape, method of producing the given product or effect and the cost of machines are not regarded as relevant. To justify a recommendation for remission of the protective duty, it must be shown that the foreign machine has a definite and marked superiority in performance over any comparable machine procurable in the United Kingdom.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are decisions made by the treasury of the United Kingdom, just as decisions under this measure are to be made by the minister of national revenue. This is described as ushering in the rule of tyranny. Well, Mr. Speaker, if any hon. member's judgment has gone so completely astray, has turned to such irrational lengths then he must, if he is to be consistent, say that tyranny has come in the United Kingdom.
Hon. members opposite do so much dislike to be reminded that there are in this country statutes, most of which were enacted in the days when hon. members opposite were in the government, conferring upon ministers and particularly upon the minister of national revenue just such necessary powers as this present bill proposes to confer upon the minister, and without appeal. These are powers without appeal.
I hold in my hand a list of these statutory measures, measures passed by this parliament conferring upon, in this case the minister of national revenue, powers by the dozens that are not subject to appeal, and practically all these statutes were enacted when a Liberal government was in power. Here they are, Mr. Speaker: The first is the Customs Act, and here we have amendments running back over these recent years. They read: the minister may prescribe; the minister may prescribe; the minister may determine value. Here, we are back in 1921 and we find that the minister may revoke a custom house broker's licence; 1951, the minister may appoint a commissioner, and so on it goes. In 1927 we find this: the minister may make regulations.
Then, there is the Customs Tariff, the statute which is now being amended; in 1948, the minister may determine the tariff or surtax; 1948, the minister may authorize collections of special duties; 1931, the minister may dispose of prohibited goods; 1950, the minister may apply specific duties to fruits and vegetables; 1931, the minister may make marking regulations.
Here is the Excise Act, and in 1934, the minister may refuse to issue a licence; 1934, the minister may prescribe; 1934, the minister may refuse a licence; 1948, the minister may require additional data, and so on it goes, the minister may prescribe; the minister may revoke penalties. Throughout all these statutes, there is no right of appeal. Practically every
Customs Tariff
one of these powers was conferred by parliament on the minister of national revenue when a Liberal government was in office. Are they going to say that there was a crisis in every year when these statutes were passed by parliament conferring these powers upon the minister without appeal? I suppose it is futile to look for anything in the way of rational argument or consistency on the part of hon. members opposite.
Let hon. members recall what happened in 1947. These great apostles of freedom, these defenders of parliament, who are they, Mr. Speaker? They are the people who in November, 1947, did not even wait for parliament to be called but announced the budget over the radio and proceeded to impose tariff embargoes and other imposts by radio without parliament even being in session. The Leader of the Opposition was not then a member of the government. However, the hon. member for Laurier was a member of that government, as was the hon. member for Essex East. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was then serving in his other political capacity as secretary of the cabinet, and was doing things in secret, as we were told this morning.
I am sure the minister does not wish to be inaccurate. I was not the secretary of the cabinet at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I apologize for having advanced the hon. member prematurely. He had not even got that far at that time.
In 1947, they proceeded to apply licences. They cut off a lot of imports, just by order in council, and in many cases nobody was permitted to import except under licence. Of course, the power to issue a licence was conferred upon the minister. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the kind of conferment of power that they view now with such stricken horror was conferred at that time upon the minister of finance. Was there any right of appeal provided from the decision of the minister of finance? There was not. Here, in case after case we have a measure applicable not simply to a handful of commodities but literally hundreds and hundreds of commodities, and there was no right to import except where the minister, in his sole discretion, directed that a permit might be granted. We are asked now to take seriously these roars and thunders from hon. members opposite in their hollow pretence that now the foundations of freedom are being shaken by this measure because it does not provide that in three simple respects in which it is so appropriate, proper and necessary that a decision be made by the minister, there is being provided no right of appeal to the tariff board. Did you ever

Customs Tariff
hear a more hollow presentation than was made today by hon. members opposite on this subject?
Then, in 1948, parliament passed the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act. It received assent on March 24, 1948. Here we find a Liberal government asking parliament to confer on a minister powers like these. Section 3: The minister may issue, vary or revoke permits for the import of such goods. Was there a right of appeal? No, there was not. Section 4 says that no permit shall be issued for the import of goods listed in schedule I, unless in the opinion of the minister, etc. Was there any right of appeal from the decision of the minister? No, there was not. Freedom must have been tottering that day, Mr. Speaker.
Then, section 6 states that, subject to this act and the regulations the minister may (a) prescribe the procedure, (b) prescribe the forms, and do all kinds of things such as (d) authorize persons in his behalf to do things. Was any right of appeal provided there? No, there was no right of appeal.
Let us look at section 12 and compare that with these protestations of hon. members opposite of their undying fidelity to the principles of the bill of rights. Section 12 provides that:
"Where a person is charged with an offence under this act, if it is established that the said person did any act for which a permit is required under this act, it shall not be necessary to establish that the person charged did not possess a permit and the burden of proof that he possessed the necessary permit shall be upon the person charged."
Well, freedom must have been shaken to its foundations that day.
Perhaps I have said enough on this subject. I pass from my comments on this aspect of the matter, Mr. Speaker, only for the purpose of reading one out of many comments that might be chosen at this point. 1 quote:
The budget proposals changing definitions of "made in Canada" will permit the manufacture here of many products now imported and will give our manufacturers a better relative position against foreign competition.
This sounds like a very sensible and fair observation as to the effect of this measure. It is interesting to know who says this. This statement appears, if you please, in a pamphlet issued by the North American Fund of Canada Limited and it is entitled, "Annual Report to Shareholders, December 31, 1960". You will observe that this annual report was issued very shortly after the introduction of the supplementary budget. Then, we find a message to the shareholders signed by the chairman and president, and it is this message to the shareholders from which I have read this particular extract. But, Mr. 
Speaker, if you are interested further and happen to turn the page you would see, under the list of officers and directors, that among those is "A. Bruce Matthews, vicepresident and director". Mr. Matthews is a very distinguished citizen and a former president of the national Liberal federation. But, Mr. Speaker, I hope you would not stop your reading there because if you were interested to go a little further and happened to read the names appearing under the list of other directors you would find there, to your shocked amazement I am sure, the name "Hon. Lionel Chevrier, Member of Parliament".

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

Look and see how he
blushes now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not in the least.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I turn to the other point. I was not a little surprised to hear hon. members opposite in both the old and new wings of the opposition say what they said today in relation to the fact that the amendment before us was proposed by the Senate. If one had reached the point of looking for nothing resembling consistency on the part of hon. members opposite, then, of course, there would be no occasion for surprise. But as to those who think hon. members of this house made in 1959 bold statements of their principles and positions on such matters, surely we are entitled to be somewhat surprised when they take a complete somersault in July, 1961.
Mr. Speaker, this is a money bill. It is a money bill under every definition of the rule respecting the prerogatives of the House of Commons in such matters. This is a money bill within the meaning of rule 63 of the standing orders of this house. This is a money bill within all of the declarations in relation to the prerogatives of this house in such matters.
We shall not be lightly misled, I am sure, in this house by the suggestion that was made, I believe by the hon. member for Ottawa West, that there was something different about the bill in 1959, on which this house took a stand in relation to this principle. I say again that in relation to this principle there is no difference whatsoever between the issue that was presented to this house in July, 1959, and the issue that is presented to it today by this Senate amendment.
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

On July 18, 1959, having regard to what is recorded in the Votes and Proceedings of this House of Commons and the minister's remarks on that day recorded in Hansard, will the minister not say that there was involved there an important difference in the ways and means in regard to the income of the crown and the taxation right of the crown on a taxpayer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say certainly not, Mr. Speaker. There is no difference whatsoever in relation to the principle at stake on this amendment today. What we had before us then was a bill to amend the Income Tax Act; and, as I pointed out this morning, the amendment did not relate to any clause respecting a rate of taxation; not at all.
No; to an imposition or not on a taxpayer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was an amendment about closing a particular class that was created by one section of the bill which did not for this purpose name rates. This was a question of closing a class of corporation and of saying that no more corporations should be permitted to qualify for that particular treatment. Was that any more of a money bill than the one we have before us today? Of course it was not, Mr. Speaker. The thing that determines what is a money bill or determines the application of the principle here involved to the amendment, is whether the main bill is in its nature a taxing statute. Does it relate to money? Is it a fiscal measure? Does it bring into effect any question pertaining to the balance of ways and means? You have these determinations, Mr. Speaker, that it is not simply appropriation acts or simply estimates that are deemed to be money bills of this house for that purpose. It is the taxing statutes, measures like the Income Tax Act as in 1959 or the Estate Tax Act as in 1958. These are money measures for this purpose; and bills to amend such statutes, are money bills and there can be no escape from that fundamental position. It is a well established position in the jurisprudence of this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Try to sell that somewhere else.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will come to hon. members opposite in a moment. What did we find in July, 1959? Mr. Speaker, when we dealt with this subject on July 18, 1959, it fell to my lot to present to the house an amendment similar in certain respects to the one now under debate or at least a message to the Senate similar to the one now under debate. There were more clauses. The third one contains these words:
The said amendment of the Senate infringes the sole and undoubted right of the Commons to impose taxation: it alters the application of taxes and interferes with the public revenue.
Customs Tariff
But this one does not involve a change in revenues.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was adopted by this house on July 18, 1959. What was said on that occasion? Both on that occasion in my own remarks and in the remarks of other hon. members on that occasion reference was made to some of the great statements of the past. In his speech on July 14, the Prime Minister had occasion to refer to remarks made in this house by some of the leading authorities of earlier years. He drew attention to what had been said on September 7, 1917. Here is what the Speaker of that day said:
On a previous occasion when this motion was under consideration, two points of order were taken by the hon. the leader of the opposition, (1) that the Senate has no power to amend a money bill, and, (2) if the Senate makes such an amendment, in view of rule 78, the house is bound to insist on its privileges and reject the amendment.
The leader of the opposition who is referred to by the Speaker in this passage is none other than Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The Speaker proceeds:
As to the first point, it is beyond question that, in view of section 53 of the British North America Act, bills appropriating any part of the public revenue or for imposing any tax or impost must originate in the House of Commons; and there is no doubt that the Senate has neither power to increase the tax or impost nor to change the incidence of the burden of any such tax or impost in any such bill originating in this house;-
And so on.
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will accept questions when I have finished if the hon. member does not mind.
Very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then further, the Speaker had something to say and Sir Wilfrid Laurier commented on the ruling of the Speaker, and asked that the remarks of the Speaker be not simply a matter of record but should be made a part of the decision of the house. That was the doctrine that was honoured by the Liberal party. In bygone years my predecessor, Mr. Ilsley, was very punctilious in his insistence on the prerogatives of the House of Commons in this matter. In 1941 when the house agreed to accept an amendment he was very careful to insist that the following should be made a part of the decision of the house. He moved:
That the said amendment be now read the second time and concurred in; but that this house, while disapproving of any infraction of its privileges or rights by the other house, in this case waives its claims to insist upon such rights and privileges but the waiver of such rights and privileges is not to be drawn into a precedent; and, further, that this house agrees to the incorporation in this bill-

Customs Tariff
Et cetera. Mr. Ilsley was very careful to insist upon that assertion of the rights of the house.
We come along to July 18, 1959. As to the nature of the measure, I simply observe that it was a measure comparable in all respects, for this purpose, with what we have before us today.
Will the minister read Votes and Proceedings of that day at page 750?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
These are the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier on September 7, 1917. This is the great voice of liberalism, Sir Wilfrid Laurier; not the hollow voices of the liberalism of 1961. He said, as quoted on page 6402 of Hansard:
It is a well-known principle that the upper chamber can reject any bill, even though it deals with financial matters, that has been passed by this house. The Senate can reject the supply bill; it can reject a bill adopted by the committee of ways and means of this house, but it cannot amend such bills.
This principle has been affirmed over and over again. Mr. Speaker, can you find a clearer statement anywhere? That was the great voice of liberalism in 1917, but that voice has been forgotten; it is not heard today by, hon. members opposite over the clamour and roar of lesser voices. On that occasion the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) chose to make some remarks following those which it had been my honour to make. They appear on the same page. He almost went so far as to congratulate the government for the strong stand it had taken in rejecting the amendment proposed by the Senate. He said:
We are therefore naturally gratified that the government has taken this position and we will support it.
That was the Leader of the Opposition on July 18, 1959, Mr. Speaker. I do remember, when that address to the Senate was adopted unanimously that day, the congratulations that were extended to the government by hon. members of the C.C.F. party. 1 can well remember the spirited applause that some of them extended to the government because we would not yield or compromise on this principle that the Senate cannot amend a money bill.
I was shocked today to hear the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) making compromise with the principles of the past. I was more shocked by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), for whom many of us in this house have great respect, this afternoon making compromise with a sound and well established principle.

These hon. members have been greatly misled since the days when they took their stand on principle in 1959.
Let us go to the people with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this points to the sorry departure of hon. members opposite from the positions they were prepared to take when they were on sound ground and stood on principles. Do not take my word for this principle-
You are right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-on which the C.C.F. stood, Mr. Speaker. Here are the words of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), then the leader of the C.C.F. party. I quote from page 5980 of Hansard of July 14. Here he was chastising the Liberal party in this house for the weakness of its position on this question. He said:
I do not think we can emphasize too strongly that with regard to money bills it should be the sole right of the House of Commons not only to originate them but in fact to have them passed in their original form.

But there is no money involved in this amendment.
Mr. Fleming (Eglinion: That was the hon. member for Assiniboia in 1959, standing on principle. Today we have the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Kootenay West leading themselves, and we do not know yet how many others, into error because they are prepared under these circumstances to depart from a sound principle. Mr. Speaker, the government stands on the principle that the Senate cannot amend money bills.
Give us an election on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution now presented is that which annually precedes the introduction of the Canadian National Railways Financing and Guarantee Act. In accordance with the practice followed since 1952, the 1961 act will again include the financing of all capital expenditures whether authorized in the current year's act or in earlier financing and guarantee acts.
The bill is intended to accomplish six main purposes. The first is to authorize the Canadian National Railways to incur capital expenditures not exceeding $178,900,000 during the 1961 calendar year.
The second is to authorize the company to make, prior to July 1, 1962, such capital expenditures as may be necessary to discharge obligations incurred under the 1961 act, but which become due for payment after January 1, 1962, as long as these expenditures do not exceed $76 million.
The third purpose served by the bill is to authorize the railway company to enter into contracts prior to July 1, 1962, for new

equipment and for general additions and conversions where payment will come due after the calendar year 1961, provided that such amounts do not exceed $44 million.
In addition to these three purposes, all of which are similar to those of previous years' acts it is necessary this year to introduce three new provisions pending a review of the Canadian National Railways capital structure. As I announced in the house last year during the debate on the financing and guarantee act, 1960, the government had intended to proceed with the re-examination and, if necessary, revision of the capital structure of the railway company prior to December 31, 1961. However, since the complete report of the royal commission on transportation has not yet been received it was considered advisable to make provision in the 1961 act for a one-year extension of the present capital structure. As the president of the C.N.R. indicated in the recent hearings before the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping, the capital structure is at present under study. This review will be continued in the light of the complete report of the royal commission once it has been received.
Consequently, the bill provides for the continued purchase by the Minister of Finance of Canadian National Railway 4 per cent preferred stock through to the end of the calendar year 1962. Hon. members will recall that the 1960 financing and guarantee act extended to December 31, 1961 the expiry date of the authority granted by the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act for the purchase of such stock up to the limit of 3 per cent of the company's gross revenue. The 1961 act will extend this expiry date by a further year.
The bill also will extend by one year, to December 31, 1962, the moratorium on interest on the government loan of $100 million to the railway company authorized by the capital revision act, 1952.
Finally, the bill will contain a new section to increase to $230 million the limitation in the Canadian National Railways Refunding Act, 1955, placed on the authority to refund maturing or matured securities of the railway company. The limit is at present $200 million and it is necessary to increase this limit to allow the refunding of securities of the company maturing during the currency of the 1961 financing and guarantee act and pending the review of the capital structure.
The financing, either by means of the issue of new securities by the government of Canada or by way of direct loan, which parliament is being asked to approve, is an

amount not to exceed $76,800,000. I would ask permission at this time to place on Hansard for the convenience of hon. members a table giving details of this amount.

As in previous years, the bill provides authority to make temporary loans to the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines to meet deficiencies in operating revenues up to June 30, 1962. As hon. members are aware, these loans to the two companies on income deficit account are of a temporary nature to meet deficiencies in revenue which regularly occur in the early part of each calendar year and are repaid later in the year either from revenues or, if these are insufficient, are written off by parliamentary appropriation. For 1961, the railway company has forecast a deficit of $64 million, while the air line is budgeting for a surplus of $500,000.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are a number of points I should like to make in connection with this legislation. In the first place, as the minister has indicated, this is the resolution which precedes the annual bill concerning the financing of Canadian National Railways. As is the custom, this bill is generally brought in after the report of the committee on railways, air lines and other government owned corporations is received. However, such is not the case this year.
I must immediately indicate to the com mittee the delay on the part of the government in connection with this matter, as in so many other matters. It has been the custom, as the committee knows, to deal with the affairs of Canadian National Railways long before the end of the session. My recollection is that in years previous to 1961, the committee on railways, air lines and shipping has reported much earlier than on this occasion. I believe

Canadian National Railways they have reported in March and April, but I have no recollection, during the long years I have been in this house, of an occasion when the committee has held its sittings so late and at this time has not brought forward a report.
When the Minister of Finance introduced a similar bill on June 7. 1960, he had this to say as reported at page 4601 of Hansard:
It is the custom to introduce this present measure after such a committee has conducted that review of the operations and financing of the Canadian National Railways system and has made its report to the house.
The question I put to the minister, then, is why is the measure being brought in before that committee has made its report?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member understands that I am not a member of that committee, but I am told the reason the report has not been made is that the chairman is ill. It is hoped the report might be submitted tomorrow morning.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not going to let the minister get away with that statement. While it is true the chairman is ill, there is a deputy chairman of the committee and there always has been a deputy chairman of the committee. The real reason is that the government could not make up its mind as to when it was going to call this committee. The real reason is that the government allowed charges to be made against the president and other officers of Canadian National Railways, and held a debate here for days during which attacks were made on the president, thereby delaying the setting up of this committee. This is the real reason we have not received a report as yet.
The custom which the minister says has been established is not being followed. However, he need not tell the house or tell me that this failure is the result of the illness of the chairman. We all regret his illness. I must say the chairman of the committee has done a magnificent job in trying to maintain order and decorum in the committee. All of us who sit on this side of the house, as well as those sitting on the other side, regret his illness. However, I come back to the point that there is a deputy chairman. There is no reason why this committee could not have been set up much earlier, and therefore had a report before us prior to the introduction of this resolution.
The other point I wish to make is this. Before we vote on this resolution, before we vote these huge sums of money to the Canadian National Railways, we should know who the directors of the railway are going to be. We had a bill introduced into this house some weeks ago increasing the number of directors


from seven to 12. Notwithstanding our demands, both prior and since the introduction and passage by this house of that legislation, we have not been able to find out who the president and directors of the Canadian National Railways are. Before we are asked to vote these large sums of money, I think it is an insult to this house not to tell us who these directors are going to be. It is of the essence of good business, good administration, for the shareholders of any corporation to be told who the directors are going to be. After all, we have a right to know what kind of people they are. We have a right to know whether or not the public will have confidence in them. We have a right to know what business experience, and the like, they have. We are not even being given that information, although the bill concerning the directors has been approved by both houses of parliament for many days, if not weeks. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that we are entitled to obtain this information before we vote these large sums of money.
There is another point which I think should be brought to the attention of the committee. This has to do with one of the subsidiaries of Canadian National Railways, namely Trans-Canada Air Lines. We were told in the committee that it was not possible to discuss certain matters affecting Trans-Canada Air Lines because they were under study by the cabinet. We were told in the committee that these matters had not been determined by the cabinet, were of a highly confidential nature, and so it was possible to discuss them. We respected the statement which was made by the minister because that has been the practice.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member precisely what matters he is mentioning. I did not ask the committee not to discuss any matters because they were before the cabinet.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I am referring to the international routes of Canadian Pacific Air Lines and those of Trans-Canada Air Lines, as well as the domestic routes. When we got to the point in committee that we were about to ask questions concerning these matters, we were told that they were sub judice; we were told that they had not been determined by the cabinet and therefore it would not be advisable to discuss them. I, for one, respected that decision. So, I say now-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: On a question of privilege-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
