speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member says that the committee was told by the minister that the

committee was not to discuss certain matters because they were before the cabinet and therefore were sub judice. I say that, as minister, I did not say that at all. When this subject was raised, I said that these matters were before the cabinet. I did not tell the committee not to discuss these matters, and I did not say they were sub judice. Any member of the committee was free to discuss any matter as long as he wanted.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister has just
confirmed what I have said; the minister is not disagreeing with anything that I have said. I am the one who said that the matters were sub judice, but the minister rose and said they were under consideration by the cabinet. He certainly made that statement, and immediately he made that statement it was quite clear that the officers were not going to give any information concerning those routes.
The point I am making now is this. Because of that statement we respected the views that were expressed then and we did not pursue the matter. Certainly, I did not pursue the matter. I say now we have arrived at another stage. Where we require large sums of money, we should be told what the position is in so far as these international routes are concerned. Is that decision going to be withheld from the committee and from the country until such time as the house has adjourned its proceedings or prorogued, for that matter, in view of what the Prime Minister said a little earlier? Then, when this house is no longer sitting will we get, as we have in the past, a statement from the Minister of Transport that here are the matters that were under review and here are the decisions that have been taken?
But the press, however, has given some indication of what is being demanded: first, that on its polar routes from Australasia via Edmonton to Amsterdam, C.P.A. be given the right to come down at London; and next, that it also be given the right to fly Toronto-Montreal by way of London with propeller aircraft. The press has given indication that those are the applications that have been made to the cabinet under the Aeronautics Act. It has been well known for many months that this matter has been under cabinet consideration. When is the cabinet going to hand down its decision? What is the nature of the application?
Before these large sums of money are voted by this House of Commons surely we should be given some indication of (1) what the applications are; (2) what effect they will have on the financial position of T.C.A.; and (3) what the decision is going to be. The same thing applies to the transcontinental air routes
Canadian National Railways now being serviced by both these large corporations which are competing with each other and unquestionably causing each other financial harm. I think the committee again in that field is entitled to know what the position is.
The minister made a statement, unfortunately not in the house, having to do with regional carriers, as he had a perfect right to do; and at least in the field of regional carriers we know what the position is east of Oshawa and Sarnia. For instance, the statement was made that applications had been filed with the air transport board relative to Quebecair, Nordair and Maritime Central air lines and the air transport board handed down its decision with reference to these matters. The minister made a statement and, at least in so far as the regional carriers are concerned, we know where we stand and the air carriers know as well. Not so, however, in the other two fields. Not so, however, in the field of international carriers and in the field of domestic carriers as well.
We also know that since the committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and operated by the government has been sitting, a team of experts from the Department of Transport have gone to Washington. What have they gone there to do? They have gone there to negotiate with their United States counterparts a renewal of the bilateral air agreement between Canada and the United States. We asked questions of the minister in so far as that matter was concerned and we received very unsatisfactory replies. However, we obtained from the press a statement by a United States delegate that it was difficult to decide on the nature of the demands and the discussions when it was impossible to find out what was in the minds of the Canadians. Of course, I am now paraphrasing a question which I put to the minister on an earlier occasion.
What did the Canadian delegates go to Washington to discuss? I think this House of Commons is entitled to know since we are voting large sums of money for this purpose. Was it to seek additional transborder routes? Was it to obtain additional routes from Montreal to Los Angeles, or from Montreal-Toronto to Miami, for instance? They are routes which we should have had since this government has been in office but which we have not obtained. Is it to offset the loss of routes which this government has granted to foreign countries by the signature of bilateral air agreements with, for instance, Italy, west Germany, France and one other country the name of which escapes me for the moment? I think the committee should be given information on matters of this kind. We have not been able to get it in the house by way of

Canadian National Railways questioning. We have not been able to get it in the committee. Surely we should be given it on this last occasion which we shall probably have to discuss matters concerning T.C.A. and the C.N.R.
It is a well known fact that Lufthansa, Air France, and Alitalia have fifth freedom rights in Montreal, with onward rights for these foreign air carriers to Los Angeles and to San Francisco and also that B.O.A.C. has fifth freedom rights to land in Toronto, something which our carriers do not possess in these countries. It is quite clear that the United States has given these foreign countries certain rights which Canada does not possess.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Who made the last agreement with the United States? What government did that?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The minister asks who made the last agreement with the United States. I do not know when the last agreement was made. However, if the minister is referring to agreements which were made when we were in office, let me tell the minister that when we gave a quid we got a quo in return and we never gave fifth freedom rights without getting from these foreign countries similar fifth freedom rights in return therefor. Not so since this government has been in office. I have not the statements before me now but I put them on Hansard last year; and I am only summarizing the position as I can but do on a measure of this character. However, there is no doubt that to west Germany, Italy and one if not two other countries went fifth freedom rights in this country in exchange for third freedom and fourth freedom rights in those foreign countries. Now an attempt is being made by the Canadian team in going to Washington to recapture the position lost in those negotiations.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: By the government of which the hon. gentleman was a member.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I think either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Transport or someone on behalf of the government should give some indication of what it was the Canadian team was seeking in Washington, what success it has had, and what was the nature of the discussions. After all, there is nothing secret about this matter. These transborder routes have been public knowledge to both Canadians and Americans for many years now. It is only fair and right that we on this side of the house and the public should know what the position is with reference to the transborder routes.
There are other matters affecting the Canadian National Railways with which I should like to deal but the amount required in this

resolution and the details thereof have just a short time ago been handed to me by the minister. On short notice like this it is difficult to deal with the matter in the manner in which I should like to deal with it at the present time.
I think those of us who sit on this side of the house will approve of the three new provisions which were announced by the Minister of Finance concerning certain extensions having to do with the capital revision of the Canadian National Railways pending a review of the capital structure of the C.N.R. by the royal commission on transportation.
I do not wish to enter into a discussion of the report of the royal commission. That has been done previously. Until the second and third reports, if that be the case, are brought down it perhaps would not be appropriate at this time to deal with that matter. However, the president of the Canadian National Railways did tell us that there was under consideration with the government at the present time a review of the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. There is no doubt that the railways all across this country-not to mention railways in the United States and elsewhere-because of competition emanating from air lines, trucks and motor vehicles, are in difficult financial circumstances. The Canadian National Railways is no exception.
The president of the Canadian National Railways gave an excellent summary of the reasons why the net revenue of the railway was so much lower this year than it has been in the past. If one gives heed to the reports that have appeared in the press from time to time, in so far as Canadian National Railways is concerned, the situation certainly is not improving. I hope the royal commission on transportation will make recommendations which the government will find it possible to adopt which will assist Canadian National Railways in the difficult financial position in which it finds itself.
There are many other things I should like to inject into the debate, but I should like to conclude on the note with which I began. It is that before we are asked to vote these huge sums of money the house should be taken into the confidence of the government and parliament should be told who are going to be the directors of Canadian National Railways and, by inference, some of the directors of Trans-Canada Air Lines also. Until we are given that information the house, in all decency, should not be asked to adopt this resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the Prime Minister's indication this afternoon that we are on the lip of an election, if one

could put it that way, I suppose every time one gets up one is conscious that this may be the last opportunity to express opinions, and especially on an institution such as the Canadian National Railways.

speechtext: Don't get political.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The Canadian National Railways bill, as has been pointed out by both previous speakers, is a routine measure in a sense. We find nothing contentious in the measure itself and are prepared to support it.
However, it does seem to me most unfair that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Transport have not taken the trouble to discover whether the report of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping will be available to the house tomorrow. Without that report before the house we are not in a position to discuss many of the points that really need to be discussed and examined which affect this resolution and the whole financial picture of the C.N.R.
The minister himself indicated that before our committee Mr. Gordon mentioned that completely new proposals with regard to the capital revision of the C.N.R. were under way or were being studied at the present time. To say they are completely new is an understatement. As far as I am concerned they are a bombshell, and I am sure they are a bombshell to the minister. They are a bombshell the size of $700 million or $900 million apparently. We cannot really discuss that now, Mr. Chairman, because in order to do so we should be able to go into the committee proceedings and, according to procedures of the house this is not allowed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member will agree with me that the proposed changes in the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways are not involved in the present bill. That is something for further study. The bill will simply continue the existing arrangement for another year to enable that study to be carried on. There is nothing in the bill that relates to that study or prejudices the right of any hon. member to comment on it in due course.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I agree with that particular aspect of it, but I say to the minister this. We have a senior management that has been in charge of the railway for 12 years. In 1950 a royal commission made certain recommendations with regard to the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. In 1952 there was a recapitalization, as the minister knows, but that measure is coming to an end and will be continued in this bill.
Canadian National Railways
To speak properly to this matter we should be able to examine wholly, in relation to this bill, the proposals and information that the president of the Canadian National Railways gave us. The minister mentioned the recent royal commission. Here is a royal commission set up in 1959. It reports in the spring of 1961. Its hearings conclude in the winter of 1961. The president of the Canadian National Railways tells us in the committee that he has these great new provisions coming about, but he did not say a word of this to the royal commission on transportation. Not one thing was brought forward in that respect.
This is a most surprising state of affairs to me, that as a consequence of our last big royal commission on transportation we get a huge revision, well over half a billion dollars, in the debt structure of the C.N.R. Now we have another royal commission, and there seems to be no indication that anything is going to be done or recommended in relation to the C.N.R. debt structure. But the president has a new proposal, and it is a dandy-$700 million or $900 million. I hope that after the resolution is passed we do not deal with the bill until we have the committee report in the house and are free to go into details of the evidence that was presented to the committee.

-I suggest that we put it to the voters of Burnaby-Richmond, because I imagine there are some people out there who will be voting in the next election and who might consider that you can link up the adjective "good" with the word "socialist". They may have something to say about the hon. member's return here.
Surely the point in regard to the directors is that the house did act to provide more directors. The official opposition took one position on it; we took another. We were glad to see the number of directors increased. But the delay is just another example of what we have come to assume is the chief characteristic of the present administration and, that, in its simplest terms, and in a word with a Latin root which would appeal to the Minister of Finance, is, simply, procrastination. When we look at this mob around us of 200 plus, we conclude it is easy enough to find Conservative M.P.'s; but it is too bad that in this mob of Conservatives in the country who stand behind them they cannot come up more quickly with people who want to be directors of this crown corporation.
The aspect of the Canadian National Railways about which I should most like to speak-but again, until we have permission to go into the evidence, it would be incomplete-is the question of whether we can have any great confidence in the present management of the Canadian National Railways. I am not going to anticipate what opinion the committee of the house which has looked at the railway might have, but it certainly is apparent from the resolution and from what the hon. member for Laurier called the vast sums involved that we are continuing to give a very free hand to the management

of the Canadian National Railways in its programs of capital expenditure.
I hope that at some time in this debate the Minister of Transport will get up and give us a review of all the capital that has been pumped into the C.N.R. in the past decade and tell us the government's view as to how effective these expenditures have been in terms of operating revenue, operating profits or losses, as they may be, and also in terms of what these capital expenditures have done in providing job opportunities. It seems to me that if we are going to have an election very soon we must look even here at one of the fundamental issues which is going to appear at that election. That is not the issue of Senate reform, but the issue of unemployment. Here is a wonderful example of what has taken place in Canadian industry. Governments, both Liberal and Conservative, supported by all parties in the house, have pumped multimillions of dollars into the Canadian National Railways for change. Out of that change they have had a reduction in jobs and job opportunities which is astounding, and if it continues at the present rate, the railways, within about four more years, will have approximately half the number of employees that they had a decade ago, that is, in about 14 years practically half of the railway labour force will have gone. We should be conscious when we are putting through expenditures on this scale that these are some of the results that are accruing to the Canadian economy.
Someone suggests that you cannot move the clock back, that we cannot be an anachronism in the railway business. One can readily agree, but when one examines the consequence of this job reduction and job dislocation which has happened with the Canadian National Railways and other railways it certainly seems that we are not geared in relation to our willingness to spend on the C.N.R., to take care of the dislocation and the lack of jobs which result from the expenditures.
We shall support the bill and we look forward to the resolution having a quick passage through the committee, especially in view of the indication that tomorrow we shall have both the bill and the report of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping before us.
The hon. member for Laurier went into some detail about the issue of Trans-Canada Air Lines and its position, especially with relation to rights which are being negotiated with the United States. What we are most concerned about is the apparent hesitancy on the part of the government and the Minister of Transport to come up with a clear-cut answer, yes or no, to the Canadian Pacific Airlines request for added opportunities for

service on the domestic lines. Again, even the friends of this government suffer from procrastination. In this regard, Trans-Canada Air Lines has given an indication that what competition was allowed on domestic routes has led them to have the first deficit in a period of nine years. We can only assume that this deficit results from the change in government policy which was made several years ago following the Wheatcroft report and the decision to allow Canadian Pacific Airlines to get into the trans-continental service. The issue is an extremely simple one and it can be put in the form of a question: Will a government decision to give Canadian Pacific Airlines more opportunity for domestic service create a greater deficit and greater problems for the government owned railway? It is as simple as that. It seems to be such a simple problem that it takes a great deal of time for the government to make up its mind. There is a very crude expression that one cannot use in the house in relation to this kind of proscrastination, but something needs to be done immediately, and since the next election is being fought on the basis not only of Senate reform, we hear, but on the basis of free enterprise versus socialism we can only assume that the government, when it finally does get through procrastinating is going to give Canadian Pacific Airlines exactly, or most of, what it is asking for.
I hope the government is consistent in its philosophy-and it seems to think it has a philosophy in this regard-because it would give us the opportunity of pointing out how paradoxical and ridiculous it is to create an instrument of national policy which is an efficient organization and then to turn around and cut its throat.

We know that the Minister of Finance in the presentation of his budget this year has done an unprecedented thing. He has not been prepared to date to inform hon. members

what the gross national productivity in 1961 is likely to be based on real values. However, we have some evidence that the Minister of Finance has not been very helpful to the House of Commons or to the country when an opportunity is given to look at the evidence concerning perhaps the biggest corporation in this country, namely the Canadian National Railways. We find that in 1961 they do not expect their revenues to increase even at the rate mentioned by the minister in his budget speech, namely 3 per cent, notwithstanding that certain costs of operation, in the opinion of the president, might be considerably greater than they were in 1960. These are questions of moment and importance which we are denied the opportunity to discuss on the grounds of a technicality, namely, that the report of the committee of 1961 has not been presented to us.
Let me use my own words. I am not going to quarrel with the president of the C.N.R. I quarrelled with him last year when he gave evidence on this same type of legislation. I said the deficit would be three or four times what it was represented to us by the government it would be and I proved to be right. This time I am only going to say that the president of the Canadian National Railways does not indicate that in 1961 his revenue will increase at a rate even comparable to the evasive and back-handed estimate given to us by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech on June 20 when he referred to a possible 3 per cent increase in growth.
I say these are the matters we have to consider when we are voting capital expenditures which involve interest on obligations of the C.N.R. This has continued year after year. These are the matters that are pertinent to the resolution before us which is a resolution preliminary to a bill. I repeat, I am not happy with technicalities and with amendments in language. The 1961 proposals for capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways may amount to $178 million, and no truly comparable figure is given to us as members of parliament with respect to the 1960 budget of $279 million.
Apparently under the rules I am debarred from dealing with the evidence upon which members of parliament are supposed to rely when we come to discuss the matter further. I am debarred from dealing with evidence taken in a careful way, I would imagine, detailed in seven or eight reports of committee proceedings, and I would assume that they involved two meetings a day. Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at any great length on this resolution. Indeed, it is not the type of resolution on which I would normally have had anything to say at all. Canadian National Railways I was in attendance in that committee on a day when the press states it was very dramatic. I had quite an interest in what happened there.
What I wished to speak about at the outset was, having been appointed to this committee and not having been removed from it, I have been receiving notices for the last few days about meetings of this committee in camera to prepare a report at a time when events in this house seemed to me to be of more compelling importance. We are now assured by the Minister of Finance, who although not a member of the committee seems to be better informed than some of us who are, that the committee is going to make a report tomorrow. I do not believe the hon. member for Laurier or I will have much idea what is going to be in that report, through no fault of our own. This is just another example of the way in which the affairs of this parliament have been mismanaged by the present administration ever since we came back in January.
As a result of our co-operation with the government in November, some legislation was passed because the government was caught off guard. Government members, however, did their best to filibuster their own legislation at that time. From January onward, we have had week after week, month after month of the time of this house and the committee of the whole taken up with endless repetition from hon. gentlemen on the other side. There was repeated delay of the important business and now we reach a situation where on the 151st day of the session, just two days short of the longest session in our whole history-this was Sir Wilfrid Laurier's session in 1903 when things were being done in this country and not being postponed-in which I venture to say that, apart from Mr. Coyne, Senator Courtemanche and the delayed budget, there will not be a person in this country who will remember anything that has happened in the whole of this session-

needs of the railway. We do not have it, though some members seem to think we do, for the purpose of engaging in a lot of useless recriminations about the past. I was exceedingly surprised that the right hon. gentleman raised it, but since he chose to do so I think the record should be set straight. This letter is dated Regina, Saskatchewan, July 15, 1953. It is addressed to J. G. Diefenbaker, Esq., Q.C., Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, and it reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Diefenbaker:
I have just seen reports in the Ottawa "Citizen" and the London "Free Press" of July 7 of a speech you made the previous day in St. Thomas in which you are said to have made certain statements about interference by the government with the Canadian National Railway hotel management at Winnipeg.
The London "Free Press" report also states you said there was proof-
And I underline that word "proof".
-that I had "complained" to the cabinet and to C.N.R. management about the "treatment" I got at the hotel.
You obviously have no personal knowledge of any such action and the president of the Canadian National Railways denied there had been any complaint.
I made no complaint to the cabinet or anyone else and it was only some weeks later that I made a reference to the matter at all in a private conversation with Mr. Donald Gordon in a reply to a question from him.

Business of the House
risks one has to take in this game and I take it. But I think perhaps I should read again from the letter and I hope that this time, having confessed that I wrote the letter myself, I might be allowed to read it uninterrupted. I am not going to read the first two paragraphs again but will commence with the third:
You obviously have no personal knowledge of any such action and the president of the Canadian National Railways denied there had been any complaint.
I made no complaint to the cabinet or anyone else and it was only some weeks later that I made a reference to the matter at all in a private conversation with Mr. Donald Gordon in a reply to a question from him.
Are you now suggesting I should not have told him the truth for fear someone would subsequently misrepresent what had happened for a supposed political advantage?
You are a lawyer and I assume when you tell the public you have "proof" of something you do not mean you have just been listening to gossip or hearsay.
I myself made a memorandum of my personal conversation with Mr. Donald Gordon which the prime minister-
That was Mr. St. Laurent.
-sent to Mr. J. M. Macdonnell, M.P. on March 30th last. Since that time I have seen no further reference by Mr. Macdonnell to the matter.
I have the prime minister's permission to send you the enclosed copy of this correspondence with Mr. Macdonnell and I would hope that, if you feel it necessary to refer again to my conduct, you will give the facts fully and fairly as I cannot imagine that you believe the Conservative party needs to distort and misrepresent facts to impress the public.
I am, of course, a newcomer in public life, but I would find it hard to believe that a public man with your many years of experience and your reputation would continue to repeat statements that are not true, once he was aware of the truth.
Yours sincerely,

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make the following announcement. Over the past few months, we have had discussions with the government of the province of Quebec with regard to the Soulanges canal, which has not been in use since the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. As a result of correspondence exchange with the minister of fish and game of the province of Quebec, we have agreed that the federal government would offer to sell for industrial purposes some land located along the Soulanges canal. It was also agreed that if, after a month, the offers received were considered inadequate by the federal government, the Soulanges canal would be offered to the province of Quebec. To that effect, Mr. Speaker, I have written today the following letter to the minister of fish and game, Mr. Gerard Levesque:
July 6, 1961.
Hon. Gerard Levesque,
Minister of Fish and Game,
Parliament Buildings,
Quebec City, Que.
Honourable Sir:
Further to my letters of last April 4 and May 12, concerning the Soulanges canal properties, X
wish to inform you that my department has received a few oifers from industrial and commercial firms in connection with the land and buildings at Cascade Point. Having given serious consideration to those offers, we have decided to turn them down and, as agreed with you, I am now prepared to recommend to treasury board that all the Soulanges canal properties be transferred to the province of Quebec for the nominal sum of $1, those properties to be used as a fish reserve for the people of the district.
As mentioned in my letter of April 4, my department would like to reserve itself the right to use, during the winter, the wharf situated at the entrance of the canal at Coteau Landing for the storage of the buoys used on lake Saint-Fran-eois, in the summer. My department will take the necessary steps to turn over to you the Soulanges canal properties as soon as we have received confirmation of your acceptance of this offer.
I should like this transaction to be subject to only one condition, namely the following:
We should like the province to undertake to keep in its service the few federal employees who are now looking after the maintenance of the canal.
Please accept, Sir, my best regards.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

Mr. Speaker, if I may, I should just like to congratulate the minister on the decision he has reached. In my opinion, it was the only one possible under the circumstances.
I will not indulge in political considerations since this question is now settled. I will merely add that it is unfortunate that it could not have been settled sooner.
The minister has written to the Quebec minister of fish and game to inform him that he was willing to hand over to the province the whole canal from the upper part, in Coteau, to Cascade Point.
I am sure that all members who followed the negotiations between the two governments are not only happy with the results but feel that it was the only proper thing to do under the circumstances.
I should like to thank the minister once more and to commend him for the decision he has made as to that matter.

is the reason why the clause provides that the money shall be provided as required from time to time by the board. That is the board of directors of the industrial development bank.
This money will be drawn down from time to time as the credit demands upon the industrial development bank require. The original $25 million capital, if I recall correctly, was not created at one particular time. It was created over a period of time until it reached $25 million and it has continued at that figure for some years now. But be that as it may, I do not think anyone suggests that this additional $25 million is going to be raised all at once. Therefore the clause makes provision for the payment by the Bank of Canada to the industrial development bank of the amount of such subscription-that is the additional $25 million-at such times and in such amounts as the board may determine.
What will happen is that the board of directors of the industrial development bank, as they require the money, will call on the Bank of Canada to provide this additional money by way of capital subscription. At that particular time, in the face of such a request, it will be a matter for decision on the part of the Bank of Canada as to where, out of its various assets, it shall take the money required; whether it shall take it out of its currency holdings or whether it shall raise the money by disposing of some of the assets held in its investment portfolio and using the proceeds for the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Several months have passed, Mr. Chairman, since the house gave second reading to this Bill No. C-71, an act respecting the civil service of Canada, and then referred it to a special committee for the purpose of study and report. This committee, under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond, has applied itself with great determination and patience to a very important task. I am sure that I simply voice the sentiments of all hon. members of this committee when I pay tribute and express the gratitude of hon. members to this special committee for the study that they have given to this bill.
The report of the committee is set forth at pages 723 to 727 of Votes and Proceedings for June 26, where all of the amendments recommended by the committee are to be found. The committee held many meetings. They entertained representations from all of the civil service associations and, indeed, at least several of them were heard on more than one occasion. It may be said, therefore, that the fullest hearing has been accorded
Civil Service Act
to those who are particularly interested in the provisions of the Civil Service Act. I do not need to remind the committee that a great deal of study had been expended in the drafting of this measure before it was introduced at the present session and before its predecessor was introduced in the 1960 session of parliament. The committee has added to that study one of the most intensive studies that I think has been given to any bill for many a year. All those hon. members of this house who served on that committee I think have justly earned and deserve the thanks of hon. members.
I, of course, did not attend the meetings of the committee, Mr. Chairman, except the first meeting and the last. However, I know that hon. members would wish a special word of thanks to be extended to the chairman, the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. The committee was evidently able to proceed with its duties in an atmosphere of calm and reasonableness, and much of the credit for the conduct of the proceedings of the committee is due the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond.
Now, a question may arise as to the status of the amendments proposed by the committee. I may say, Mr. Chairman, that as the sponsor of the bill in this house I am happy to accept the amendments proposed by the committee to the bill. As we proceed in committee of the whole on the clauses of the bill, the amendments will be moved to the clauses and so far as I am concerned, as sponsor of the bill, I make it very clear I am happy to accept all of the amendments proposed by the committee. I believe they do improve the bill over the form in which it was originally introduced and given second reading.
I know that all hon. members in the present deliberations of the committee of the whole will have regard for the fact that this bill has received, on the part of the special committee, a most thorough examination.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, we are presented, in the dying days of the session, with a bill that certainly does not have the urgency which is apparently being ascribed to it. Salaries were raised not so long ago, and it cannot be expected that the civil servants will have to come back to the government in the near future, something which would justify the immediate passing of this Bill C-71 before we come back in September.
However, the government has decided that this bill should be submitted to the house before adjournment. Being outnumbered, we shall have to accept.

Civil Service Act
I agree with the minister that the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Mac-Lellan) deserves to be commended for leading the committee with great intelligence and skill and for managing, despite some rather sharp differences of opinion at times, to maintain an atmosphere of harmony such as does not exist in every committee.
I must say to the minister that when the government has names to suggest for membership in committees, an effort should be made to consider personalities, but whenever we have a chairman such as the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond, we may still meet with problems but there will never be cause for bitter discussions. I therefore wish to thank the hon. member for his courtesy to all hon. members, and particularly to members of the opposition.
The committee met a number of times. We considered the bill very carefully. I must also thank those who appeared as witnesses, such as the members of the civil service commission, the representative of the treasury board and the representatives of the associations, whose specialized knowledge was very helpful. Frankly, without their assistance and support, the situation would have been extremely difficult. I want to acknowledge their ability and generosity in that regard. In some cases, we may have pressed our questions a little too far, but they always answered our questions with equal co-operation and made our task very easy.
We had a statute that had been on the books since 1918. It obviously needed revamping, because it is impossible to tell 50 years ahead of time what is going to happen.
When the first legislation was enacted, Canada was a colony and the civil service was not as large as it is now. In the meantime we had two wars, during which it was necessary to increase personnel.
Since Canada achieved independence and became a free country, our relations with other countries have been extended; this has called for the establishment of a Department of External Affairs which considerably increased the burden of the civil service as far as selection of personnel is concerned. In my opinion the act, even though outdated, has served its purpose well and, until this year, we did not have too much trouble in the matter of salaries and working conditions. This may be due to the fact that, under the previous administration, or the preceding ones, there were people in office who could

act with benevolence, who understood the workers, the needs of employees. That is why there may have been discussion with civil servants and their associations, but we never felt the need to seek a set protection provided by law, because we knew how to get along with them and granted them, if not all they were asking for, at least what they were entitled to expect from a government.
There were no secret documents at that time. There was no injustice due to delays in granting salary increases, as happened recently when employees were granted raises, between April and October, that were not retroactive. Those raises applied only from the day the department had decided to grant them, and so, for six months, some civil servants lost an increase they were entitled to expect. Why was this done? I do not know, and no explanation was ever given in that regard. I even wonder whether the minister can explain his delay in the matter.
Only this government could spoil everything and make civil servants suspicious of the government.
The new legislation certainly contains improvements. There are some items which considerably improve upon the old act; they have been seriously considered, but they do not amount to all the improvements the civil servants have a right to expect.
I have here a press release sent by the civil service association's chairman, Mr. Best. This is what he says:
(Text):
C.S.A.C. national President J. C. Best has issued the following statement dealing with the amendments to clauses 7, 10, and 69 of Bill C-71, the revised Civil Service Act. The statement has been approved by the executive committee of the association and represents the official position of the C.S.A.C. The statement said:
"The civil service association of Canada has now studied the provisions of clauses 7, 10, and 69 of Bill C-71 (the Civil Service Act) as amended by the special committee of the House of Commons on June 23. Since passage by the committee more or less assures acceptance by the House of Commons, this association now wishes to record its comments on the clauses which, unfortunately could not be made before the committee.
Generally speaking there can be no doubt that the amended clauses represent improvement over the original forms of clauses 7 and 10. However, the association and its members are disappointed that certain basic principles of our position copld not gain acceptance in the committee or from the government. We are as concerned with too rigid legislation as is the government. However, we do not feel that the position we took before the committee requesting negotiation, consultation and arbitration implied any rigidity whatsoever. We viewed these principles as minimum safeguards to the rights of civil servants.

In introducing these amendments the Minister of Finance emphasized the need for good will and good faith on the part of all concerned. With this viewpoint we can readily agree. However, we would point out that such a climate is more readily achieved if the legislation under which we work enumerates certain basic principles which, in our view, are essential to a satisfactory employer-employee relationship within the government service.
Our major area of concern is the lack of definition of what constitutes consultation and whether it is synonymous with negotiation as we view it. We are also concerned that there is no means whatsoever in the legislation to solve fundamental points of disagreement which must, from time to time, arise regardless of how much good faith is evidenced by the parties concerned. We thus feel that the refusal of some constitutionally acceptable form of arbitration will inhibit the staff associations in their representations and will provide additional strains on the "consultative process".
Our other major concern is the government's belief that after so many years we can in effect only now begin to evolve a satisfactory system of dealing between it and its employees on matters concerning salaries, wages and working conditions. In the absence of any indication as to how long the government feels such an evolutionary process should take we are deeply concerned that we may be faced with many more years of struggle to achieve what we feel are legitimate and necessary goals. We do feel that some firm indication is needed on the government's part as to how long it feels this process will take, and when the question of changing the legislation to come closer to our wishes can again expect to be raised before a parliamentary committee. We feel that three to five years is as long as we should be expected to rely on evolution, in view of the long period that has passed without significant change. While we can see validity in a program of gradualism where no precedents exist for guidance, we do not feel that this applies to the present situation.
The civil service association of Canada will do everything possible to assist in working out proper machinery under the act.
(Translation):
As you see, Mr. Chairman, the association was very willing to co-operate with the government. But civil service organizations have some misgivings. Can you blame them for it? Their representatives asked that certain basic protections be included in the legislation. They were not given satisfaction, and they have some misgivings in this respect, because, during the three or four years that this government has been in power, difficulties have always cropped up when these people tried to obtain a salary increase or reasonable working conditions.
In the first case, the civil service commission had recommended not to grant any raises in salaries. The Minister of Finance immediately informed the public of the decision that the requested increases were not being granted.
However, when, on a second occasion, the civil service commission recommended an increase to the department, which submitted the matter to the treasury board, and when an increase had been recognized aceept-
Civil Service Act
able and was to be granted, the position was quite different. Nobody in Canada knew what was going to happen. The minister kept his great secret to himself. The report was held to be a document which could not be revealed either to the house, or to the public, or to federal employees.
It was necessary to wait until the government was ready to say, in April, what categories of civil employees would benefit from a salary increase, as from the first of that month; in May, another group of federal civil servants would be granted a raise, but from May 1 and not April 1. In June, another group of civil servants would be granted an increase, but only as from June the first.
That is how the government went about it, from month to month, granting successive salary increases, but never allowing the civil servants to benefit from retroactivity to April 1, which was the date of the first increase which had been granted, so that federal employees lost some of their confidence in this government; and they can scarcely be blamed for it.
As federal civil servants stated themselves, they accepted the situation, but unwillingly. They are not satisfied with the way they were treated by the government, and they cannot be blamed for that either.
In spite of some improvements, civil servants were sadly disappointed. They had hoped to be treated as first class employees; they had hoped that, as in industry, they would be able to meet the government's representatives and discuss their working conditions and salaries man to man, and not as slaves facing a master.
But at that stage the minister decided that there should be no more than consultation, not negotiation. Those civil servants remain second class citizens, because the Minister of Finance decided that he could not grant them the right of negotiating on a basis of equality with their employer.
That is a situation which is not accepted anywhere in the world, in industry, and it is essential that the government recognize that its employees are entitled to meet their employer and to discuss their working conditions and their salaries man to man. The Canadian government had to be the first to withhold recognition of that right.
The Saskatchewan government is known to have recognized that principle. Did the

Civil Service Act
civil servants in Saskatchewan experience any difficulties? Not in the least. The government and its employees finally agreed on all points, and even if the parties concerned did not obtain all they wanted, they secured a good deal, which enabled them to accept something which did not reduce them to a subordinate standing as human beings.
Why did the federal department reject a request to negotiate? Some officials have stated that the suggestion of the minister had finally been accepted, though it was far from satisfactory, because they had no choice.
The minister indicated that the words "consultation" and "negotiation" meant about the same thing. On this subject, I have here a release issued by the federated association of mail-carriers of Canada, which states:
(Text):
The minister, in his preamble, pointed out that after consulting various dictionaries he was unable to see where the word "consultation" did not meet the same requirements as the word "negotiation". He also stated that he did not favour writing into legislation detailed provisions for negotiation and arbitration.
Whilst the amendment submitted by the minister is, to some extent, an improvement on the original draft of the proposed clause, it does not, in our opinion, give staff associations the protection to which they are entitled.
We fail to see-and we have also consulted dictionaries-where the words "consultation" and "negotiation" are synonymous; on the contrary, we find that there is a vast difference between the two.
When this association submitted its brief it did not suggest that detailed provisions for negotiation and arbitration should be written into the act; we did feel very strongly, however, that the word "negotiation" should be written into the act where it now mentions "consultation",-
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I have looked up dictionaries, and this is what I have found:
Negotiator: A person who is appointed to discuss with someone. The negotiators of an alliance.
Negotiation: The act of negotiating important public or private business. That business itself. To break off, to resume negotiations. The act of transferring, of surrendering commercial papers.
Negotiate: To carry on business. To carry on business in the east. Of commercial papers or drafts, to transfer, to pass on to somebody else. To discuss through diplomatic channels or with an individual. To be negotiated, to be the subject of negotiations.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, this is what the dictionary has to say about the word "consultation" and its derivatives:
Consultant: A person who gives advice, as a lawyer, a doctor. One who seeks a consultation.
Consultation: The act of consulting. The study of a case by one or more lawyers, of a patient by one or more doctors. Advice given by lawyers, doctors. A conference held to consider a case.

Consult: To seek the opinion of someone. To consider in order to gather information, an explanation. To consult a book. To confer, to deliberate. They are consulting each other. To give consultations. To consult oneself, to deliberate within oneself.
It can be seen that, in one case, the word "consult" means to parley, to hold parleys, while "negotiation" means to parley for a specific purpose, and it is precisely what the postal employees and employees in the other divisions of the civil service have asked for- the right to negotiate rather than the right to consult.
Besides, as far as the principle of consultation is concerned, whether the minister inserts it in the act or not he has granted nothing more to them, for there has been consultations in the past. In fact, whenever government employees have had the privilege to parley with the authorities, those of course were consultations; but that was all. They met with the authorities of the department and explained their problems. The authorities acknowledged the explanation of the problems, dismissed the employees and held discussions among themselves and the civil servants were not informed of what had happened.
On the other hand, when negotiations are held the representatives remain together to the end and they are there and know what the employer's final decision-in this case the government's decision-will be.
That is what they want to know. Therefore, there should be more co-operation between the two parties, so that the civil servants know, before being kicked out, what has been the final decision reached by the government.
They want to know where things stand and what other representations they might make in case they did not get satisfaction.
There are also a number of strange things in the bill before us.
For instance, the civil servants have asked that the word "grievance" be defined. The committee, with the support of its majority, has refused this suggestion. I later made the same suggestion myself, and was told this was not necessary, as the wording was clear enough. As a result, I have come to wonder whether lawyers do not have a special purpose in mind when they say everything is clear. In fact, I wonder if this is not a way of getting more cases and providing for longer and therefore more profitable discussions. I wonder if that could be their purpose.
The civil servants have asked for a clear definition of the word "grievance". They were told no, there was no need for that, as everyone knew what it meant.

Yet there are many definitions in the bill, but when it came to the word "grievance", the government objected.
Those people only asked that the word "grievance" be described as such. A grievance is a reason alleged for a complaint. It would have been easy for the minister to accept that the simple word grievance be defined.
It might have made the bill clearer. Perhaps it would have been repetitive. I do not think so, not being afflicted with the quirks of the legal mind. It would probably be a clarification involving repetition, as lawyers felt it was clear. It seems to me, however, that in the circumstances, the simple word "grievance" might have been made clear, as this would have clarified the bill. Besides there is always room for improving a rather confused situation.
Confidential reports and delays of applications which cause unfair losses with this new word "consultation" instead of "negotiation" will again arise. The government will again be faced with the same problems, though it can ill afford such problems.
Indeed the government does not have to wait for its pay to survive; it is not the government that suffers from working conditions; it is the employees.
The employees are the ones who suffer. They are the ones who want to remove the causes of friction and the difficulties they have been faced with, and have them replaced by smooth discussions, so that when a final settlement has been reached, they will be able to say to the government: Here is what we suggest. We have had discussions with the staff and have reached an agreement. We now ask parliament to refuse or accept the decision reached by the government as a result of discussions with its staff.
The minister has referred to arbitration. He referred to it as something highly dangerous. He said he opposed it because he wanted to protect the rights of parliament.
It is rather astonishing to hear such words from the minister-to protect the rights of parliament. Indeed, since 1958, we in the opposition have many times had occasion to complain that the rights of parliament were disregarded by this government, who often took advantage of its overpowering majority to disregard our legitimate requests, to refuse to produce documents we needed, to turn down our suggestions that matters be referred to committees, to refuse to bring forward its legislation in time so that we could study it,
Civil Service Act
to refuse to announce the business for the session.
And now the minister rises and says he wants to protect the rights of parliament.
When it comes to minor employees who cannot defend themselves, oh, they want to protect the rights of parliament. Members of parliament can easily protect themselves when their rights are interfered with.
Civil servants cannot take such steps. If they raise their voices, their employer can make trouble for them.
That is why I say the act could have been improved. Civil servants should have been given collective bargaining like provincial employees have in Saskatchewan. There has not been more trouble in that province; in fact, there has been less than here. Why?
Because that provincial government has gained the confidence of its employees, while, here, the present employees of the various services or various associations no longer trust the government. The reason is that they have been unfairly treated in the past three or four years, that is, since the present government came to power.
Parliament's rights would not be threatened if we accepted or encouraged bargaining.
The only case where the rights of parliament could be threatened would be if the minister arbitrarily decided to grant salary increases without consulting parliament or without previously asking the latter to approve the necessary funds.
When parliament is consulted with respect to decisions which have already been taken and which involve the government and some other body, be it a civil servants' organization, a provincial government or a foreign government, it cannot be said that there has been encroachment upon the fundamental rights of parliament, because in all those cases, the government has come to an agreement.
One example of that is the agreement between the Canadian government and the United States government on the South Saskatchewan river dam. Was there any encroachment upon parliament's rights because that agreement was signed before it was submitted to parliament? Did we take offence? No, because we knew that sooner or later parliament would have full opportunity to discuss it and that it would have a final say in the matter.
In this case, naturally, giving bargaining rights to employees would in no way threaten or challenge parliament's prerogatives because if there were a dispute, they would just

Civil Service Act
submit their case to an independent body which would hear the evidence and submit its recommendations to parliament. Those recommendations would either be endorsed or turned down.
There has been some talk about the employees' right to go on strike. Only one association mentioned it but did not insist.
In fact, civil servants already have that right since anything which is not specifically prohibited is permissible.
Now, nothing in the previous act prohibits civil servants from going on strike. The same situation prevails in England.
Yet, civil servants have not taken advantage of that right.
Nothing in this bill forbids employees from going on strike; therefore, they still have that right since there is no prohibition in that connection. Consequently, civil servants have the right to strike.
At any rate, that is idle talk because civil servants neither have the intention nor the desire to call a strike.
Most staff organizations, the civil service association of Canada, the civil service federation of Canada and the professional institute of the public service of Canada have stated most emphatically that they have no intention of calling strikes or of taking advantage of their right to do so regardless of whether or not it is in our statutes.
I might add1 that it is not in their interests to go on strike since they have other means at their disposal, especially if they are given bargaining rights.
Those recommendations have been turned down. Why? I could not say. Certain lawyers say that the answer is obvious even though they feel a need to discuss the point. They fear repetitions; yet, that would be conducive to a clarification of this matter.
It was said that this is obvious; still, lengthy discussions took place, questions were asked and long talks were held. However, when asked to tell exactly what would be the prevailing rates, they refused to answer saying it was clear.
There were ten members in attendance, and five of them were not of that opinion. As a matter of fact, the commission's interpretation was often at variance with that of the members of the committee.
It is quite clear that there was a lack of precision there. A text should be given the meaning it should have.

A bill does not have to be a piece of literature but still it must be clearly worded, even if repetitions are involved.
That is why it would have been better for some points to be clarified.
As far as prevailing rates are concerned, I think it was wrong not to accept the suggestions made by the spokesmen of the association.
Another feature of this act which may be criticized is the fact that it grants too full powers to deputy heads. Already those powers were not inconsiderable, yet they are further extended. The deputy heads may do as they wish in order to crush any employee they dislike, because they are sole masters according to the commission and the government. Such a situation should not exist under a civil service act.
I suggest that the powers given the deputy heads and their responsibilities should be limited; that the commission should have the last word-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. gentleman but his speaking time is up.
(Text):
Carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the committee agree that the hon. member be allowed to proceed?

Agreed.
(Translation):

Thank you, and I also thank the committee for allowing me to continue. I hope I will not be too long.
Deputy heads have powers that are too extensive while the commission gets too little.
I think that powers should be given the commission. In fact, the commission deals with individuals that it does not know. Not knowing them, it can examine the matter objectively without saying: "This is the case of So and So; I do not like the looks of him." We often meet people we dislike at first sight. Well, deputy heads are no exception. The civil service commission sends a man over but as he does not like the looks of the applicant, he sidetracks him and, at the first opportunity, the commission manages to fire him on the pretence that he does not give satisfaction. I think that deputy heads are granted too much power. I am sure that, even in the ranks of the government members, there are people who agree with me on this subject. I met some in the committee who

felt the same as I do. The powers of the deputy heads should be limited, and those of the commission should be increased, because in the last analysis, it is the commission that cannot feel any bitterness against any one.
I also think that too much power is given the governor in council. That is a natural tendency with the Tories which we cannot countenance. The governor in council reserves too many powers to himself.
When considering this bill, clause by clause, we will have an opportunity to submit amendments to this effect. That the governor in council has some rights, I admit, but those rights should be limited. They should be well defined, so as to avoid all risks of overriding the powers of some other group. That is why we should be careful when granting such extended powers to the governor in council.
Something else is lacking in this legislation, which is not made clear, because it is claimed this has been handed to the commission to draw regulations therefrom: it is the rights of appeal which are not properly defined. Even if this is included in the regulations, and even if the regulations are considered in consultation with employees' associations, I suggest it would be much clearer if it were provided in the act that certain points may constitute cause for appeal in order to protect the lower civil servant who, often, is the victim of more important people who take advantage of their position-they are those whom we usually call beggars on horseback-to oppress those around them. We often see petty officials who, having climbed the social and official ladder, lose all notions of decency and crush everyone under them. I suggest we should provide for such cases in including very definite rights of appeal in the act.
There is another case which has not been corrected, and which should have been. It is that of veterans. The protection we had provided for them, under the former act, is included in the new one. But neither the former act nor this one provide any recognition for those who served in the army but remained in Canada, against their own wishes, because their special knowledge was required for some work in Canada rather than in Europe or elsewhere. To those veterans is denied the right of preference over others. You may say: "Of course, but the others, it is them who decided to risk their lives abroad." But, they too were prepared
Civil Service Act
to go overseas to risk their lives. But they were kept in Canada because they were needed here. All the same those soldiers had some merit, but it is not recognized. A new act is enacted which completely ignores those who stayed in Canada. I claim that the government should amend the act to give those veterans some advantage, not as much as for the others, but when they pass an examination they should be allowed an advantage of 10 or 15 per cent so that they may have a better chance of being eligible for the civil service.
Those are a few of the amendments which could be moved.
However, notwithstanding the briefs of the conseil de la vie frangaise and the St. John the Baptist Society, I say that there has been no improvement introduced as far as bilingualism is concerned. Confederation is almost 100 years old and we are still treated as the poor relations of the majority. Is it normal that after some 100 years of common existence, we should still be considered as poor relatives? I would have thought that after 100 years, we should know each other well enough and understand each other well enough that prejudices would no more exist.
At present, does the bilingual individual, either French or English, have any advantage? If he is bilingual, he should be considered superior to others. We generally recognize that the minority becomes superior, and that is a necessity imposed by nature. In every country where there is a minority and a majority, we know that the minority, due to its condition, has to become intellectually superior to become the equal of the majority. That we recognize.
I am not asking that everyone learn French or that everyone learn English, but when one knows both languages, he should enjoy special consideration. I suggest that those who are bilingual should get special consideration and this would encourage the study of both languages. In fact, if in a civil service competition a candidate can say he knows the spoken language of the other part of the country if not its written one I say he should be granted at least 5 per cent more than the others who cannot do as well, so that he may have a better opportunity of earning and promotion. This would favour all those who care to study another language. Even when it is not definitely necessary, they could do it as a means of improving their cultural standards.
Besides, the hon. member from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) suggested in committee-and

Civil Service Act
I entirely agree with him-that the civil service organize both a French course and an English course for those who do not have adequate knowledge of the other language to help them to be prepared for better positions. I think that suggestion should be most seriously considered. For the time being, I will not move an amendment in that regard, because I know it would mean immediate expenditures and under the rules, I cannot move neither in the house nor in committee, an amendment that would result in an additional expenditure. But I do hope the government will continue to give consideration to that matter in order to encourage people to further their intellectual development. I am sure that by granting a 5 per cent more to those who would be able to show in a competition that they know the two languages spoken in this country, we would reach this objective. In this way, the act would be amended in such a way that everybody, and especially the civil servants, would be satisfied, because they would be the ones to suffer if the act were not satisfactory and were left as long as the old act without being amended. At that rate, many of those employees would be dead a long time before ever seeing their lot improved.
Well, I ask the government if it will consider it carefully.
As far as bilingualism is concerned, here is a recent development. Notice had been given of a promotion competition for the office of director of district No. 2 which includes part of the country of Pontiac, the counties of Gatineau, and of Hull, part of the counties of Labelle, Argenteuil, Russell, Stormont, Ottawa East and Ottawa West, as well as many neighbouring counties. There are a great many French speaking Canadians in that district, and I asked the minister why a bilingual employee was not required for that office. He replied that this was not necessary, since the district includes an important part of Ontario, and therefore a bilingual employee was not required. Nevertheless, while we are dealing with a postal district, even where post offices might not be as important as those in Montreal, Toronto or Ottawa, such opportunity could well have been taken to require that a bilingual director be appointed. Many people are qualified for that office. But no: it was decided that this was not necessary. And the minister told us the other day that the decision was the responsibility of the civil service. That statement is wrong: such decision does not come from the civil service, but from the officials of the Post Office Department who decide which qualifications will be required, and the civil service sets out its competition according to those requirements. Therefore, the

department has the right to ask for a bilingual director, be it a French speaking or an English speaking person, provided it is a bilingual employee.
When the mail-carrying service was inaugurated at Gatineau, they had to call upon a bilingual official from Montreal, because the head of the service in Ottawa could not speak French. They realized thus that bilingualism is a necessity; and yet, they did not think it advisable to remedy the situation.
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I took up more time than was kindly granted me by the house. We shall have occasion to take the matter up again and propose amendments to several clauses.
(Text):
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? Was the hon. member speaking of the civil service or of his relatives?
That is a fine question but I suggest you should direct it to the Minister of Finance, because I would not stoop that low. Some of my relatives may be in the civil service-
Some of mine are too.

Yes, some of your relatives may be in the civil service too but I am not responsible for that. I can tell you this: if some members of my family are in the civil service they are there of their own accord, because I did not give them recommendations. I can state that I do not intend to give any member of my family a recommendation for employment in the civil service.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a member of the committee I am happy to report that no such suggestion was discussed there. The proceedings of the committee were not conducted on the level of the last question.
I should like to congratulate the chairman of the committee because I think he did a good job as chairman. He understood the problems that were being discussed. He was lenient with the points of view with which he did not agree, and if there was an honest difference of opinion in the committee he was willing at all times to allow the matter to stand over to see whether some compromise could not be worked out. I think this is the kind of job that a chairman should do and I was certainly pleased to be a member of that committee. I highly recommend the hon. gentleman to the government as an excellent and capable chairman.
The remarks that I have to make cannot be made in the light of whether I have relatives in the civil service because to the best of my knowledge I have none. Very few civil

servants in my riding are in the category of office staff. With the exception of a very limited number my riding does not consist of civil servants. Therefore, I was interested in this matter not on the basis of patronage, not on the basis of what we could get out of it but rather on the basis of what we could put into the committee to accomplish what we all really want, namely the best civil service and the best possible agreement for those civil servants because this is the way to establish a very active and effective civil service body.
In my opinion the members of the civil service commission who attended on a number of occasions were very co-operative in their replies. They were willing to discuss in very broad and effective terms the matters that fell within their jurisdiction.
I agree with the previous speaker with regard to the presentation of our regional arguments having to do with improvement in the civil service. That problem still remains with us. I refer to the matter of whom the civil servants negotiate with, what type of relationship exists between the civil service commission and the civil servants themselves, the civil service associations and representations. I believe this is the crux of the disagreement between the government and the opposition. This is also the reason why the Civil Service Act was opened up at this time. As has been said, there is at the present time no disagreement over salaries or wages but there will continue to be a disagreement if the same type and method of negotiation is continued that took place at the time the civil servants received their last pay increase. I believe the civil servants themselves have the right to know with whom they negotiate, how they negotiate with whatever body is selected for negotiation and what results come from those negotiations. It is still confusing in my mind and I think in the minds of most Canadian civil servants as to whom they negotiate with.
This matter is not nearly as simple as if you were negotiating with management in a plant where you might find that the management really did not have any say because there was a board of directors over that management. But in that case you do know that the representations you make to management in those negotiations are referred to the board of directors. In the case of civil servants' negotiations I am not too sure with whom they are negotiating and I am sure that they are not. We heard such terms kicked around as the governor in council, the treasury board, the civil service commission and the parliament of Canada itself. I think that in solving some of the problems that have been apparent over the past three
Business of the House
years we will have to make a change. This is not one of the changes that has been suggested but we shall have to make a fundamental change so the civil servant and his association will know how to proceed in negotiating under the normal procedure commonly referred to in other acts administered by the federal government. I refer specifically to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
In other countries civil service commissions have been given authority to make representations in relation to pay and to other conditions of work. They make those representations after having consulted with the associations that represent the employees. When they make those representations to the government, or to the cabinet, a decision has to be arrived at at that level. The governor in council will decide on behalf of the government and of parliament what pay increases will be granted to the civil servants. But in most cases that I have examined where the commission was the equivalent to the civil service commission in Canada, those representations were made public and everyone knew what were the suggestions of the civil service commission and on what grounds the submission had been made. Thus the civil service commission retreats from the negotiations because they become political on the one hand and a matter for decision by the members of civil servants themselves through their associations. Negotiations should take place on that level. I think this has not been done by this government. It probably has not been done by any government in Canada in the past. It seems to me this is the crux of the question of a need for change in the Civil Service Act.
Will you call it 10.30, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.
